sources.claim: May Mobility runs a commercial driverless microtransit service with no operator aboard in Peachtree Corners, Georgia, using Toyota Sienna autonomous vans on public streets; the vehicles carry riders but do not assist or supervise them outside the vehicle.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: shared autonomous shuttle transport of the general public. Transfer is limited to the vehicle-driving portion of an outing; no evidence of passenger escorting, mobility assistance, or group supervision.

sources.developer: City of Detroit / May Mobility / Michigan Mobility Collaborative
sources.title: Detroit Expands "Accessibili-D" Autonomous Shuttle Routes Following Successful Initial Deployment for Seniors and Residents with Disabilities
sources.claim: Detroit's Accessibili-D autonomous shuttle service for seniors and residents with disabilities, operated with May Mobility, keeps a trained human safety operator aboard at all times specifically to help riders board and alight and to handle problems, showing that autonomous vehicles serving this rider population still depend on a human attendant for the assistance portion of the trip.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: transporting older adults and people with disabilities in the community. It is the closest deployed analogue to the outing-transport step and shows the human assistance role is retained, supporting a negative judgment.

It covers only single-rider conveyance on mapped indoor routes; it does not transfer people into or out of the chair, manage a group, or operate in uncontrolled community settings.

tasks.label: Provide emergency first aid and summon medical assistance when necessary.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Minor injury in a residence hall: a student cuts a hand, scrapes a knee, gets a nosebleed or minor burn. The RA meets them in the RA room, lounge or hallway, inspects the injury, cleans it, applies antiseptic and an adhesive bandage or gauze from the duty first-aid kit, decides whether health services follow-up is needed, and logs the incident.

Intoxicated or unresponsive student in a dorm room, bathroom or stairwell, usually at night: RA checks responsiveness and breathing, rolls the person into the recovery position, clears vomit/airway, monitors, calls 911/campus EMS, disperses peers, unlocks and props doors, and directs paramedics to the room.

Group home resident medical event in a home-like living area or bedroom: a seizure, a fall with a laceration or suspected fracture, hypoglycemia, or an allergic reaction. The advisor protects the person's head, controls bleeding, gives glucose or an epinephrine auto-injector per the care plan, manages an agitated or non-verbal resident, and calls 911 and the on-call nurse.

Life-threatening collapse anywhere in the residence (bedroom floor, bathroom, corridor, tight space between furniture): no pulse or no breathing. RA starts chest compressions and rescue breaths, sends someone for the wall AED and applies pads, or administers intranasal naloxone for a suspected opioid overdose, and continues until EMS takes over.

Incident on the grounds or just outside the building: injury at an outdoor residence event, in a courtyard, parking lot or recreation area, in variable weather and light. RA reaches the person over uneven ground, stabilizes and shelters them, controls bystanders, calls EMS and guides the ambulance in.

sources.title: For the first time in medical history, an autonomous drone helps save the life of a cardiac arrest patient
sources.claim: Everdrone's EMADE service uses autonomous drones to fly an AED to the scene of a suspected out-of-hospital cardiac arrest; in a documented Swedish case the drone-delivered defibrillator contributed to saving a patient. The drone delivers equipment only - a physician on scene performed the resuscitation - so it does not perform hands-on first aid.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: emergency equipment delivery / summoning aid. It covers only the 'summon' half of the task and the logistics of getting a device to the scene; every physical act of first aid (compressions, pad placement, airway management) was still done by a human bystander, so it cannot substantiate completion of any instance.

sources.title: Performance, Safety, and Patient Experience of an Autonomous Robotic Phlebotomy Device: A Multicenter Trial
sources.claim: The Aletta autonomous robotic phlebotomy ... inserts a needle into a patient's fixtured arm without an operator, supervised at a ratio of up to three devices per healthcare professional, in accredited outpatient phlebotomy laboratories. It is a single scheduled, fixed-geometry procedure on a seated cooperative patient.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: autonomous needle insertion on a human. It is the closest deployed case of a robot autonomously acting on a human body, but it works only on a cooperative patient whose arm is immobilized in a cuff for one pre-scripted procedure; it performs no injury assessment, no deformable-dressing manipulation, and no escalation decision, so it does not transfer to rendering first aid to an injured or collapsed person.

sources.title: Development of artificial intelligence-driven biosignal-sensitive cardiopulmonary resuscitation robot - PubMed
sources.claim: An AI-driven robot that adjusts chest-compression depth, rate and position from biosignals was shown to be feasible only as a proof of concept in anesthetized pigs on a laboratory table, with the compression device placed on the animal by researchers.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: mechanical chest compression. Even this animal-lab system does not find, approach, assess or position a collapsed human; humans mount it on an already-instrumented subject, so it cannot complete the CPR instance in any setting.

sources.system: DARPA robot medic / smart tourniquet SBIR solicitation
sources.title: DARPA launches search for robot medics to treat battlefield casualties
sources.claim: As of May 2026 DARPA was soliciting proposals to create autonomous robots able to reach casualties, assess wounds, form tourniquets and inject drugs at the point of need - evidence that autonomous robotic emergency first aid is a research goal rather than an existing capability.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: point-of-injury emergency care. This is an announcement of intent, not a demonstration; it is cited only to show the state of the art, ... per the rules it supports no positive judgment.

sources.system: Robotic wound redressing tape-handling system (dexterous hand on manipulator arm)
sources.title: Towards Autonomous Tape Handling for Robotic Wound Redressing
sources.claim: Robotic wound redressing remains a laboratory research problem: a 2025 study automates individual sub-steps of tape handling using data collected through human teleoperation of the manipulator, with degraded performance on human skin.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: applying and removing wound dressings. It is the nearest work to bandaging a wound, but it is a teleoperation-derived lab prototype covering only sub-steps, so it cannot substantiate whole-instance completion at worker quality.

tasks.label: Make regular rounds to ensure that residents and areas are safe and secure.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Overnight safety checks in a small group home or family-style residential care home (I/DD, mental health, substance-abuse recovery): every 30-60 minutes the sole staffer walks the house, enters each bedroom to confirm the resident is present and not in distress, checks exterior doors and windows secured, stove and appliances off, no hazards, and logs each check.

Rounds in a homeless shelter, transitional or supportive housing program: walk congregate sleeping bays, bathrooms, common rooms and entrances; verify curfew/headcount, look for intoxication, contraband, medical distress or conflict; make sure doors are secured; log the round.

Timed unit checks in a residential treatment, juvenile or psychiatric residential facility: visual room checks on every resident at required intervals (e.g., 15 minutes), confirming each resident's condition, scanning for ligature/self-harm hazards and contraband, verifying doors and windows secure, documenting each check.

Quiet after-hours security round of a college residence hall: walk corridors on each floor, stairwells, lounges, laundry and study rooms, check exterior and fire doors are not propped or unsecured, look for leaks, burnt-out lights, damage, smoke odor or unauthorized persons, log the round and report issues.

Residence hall or boarding-school round involving resident contact: room-by-room check-ins or lights-out verification, knocking on doors, addressing noise/alcohol violations and unauthorized guests, checking on distressed or intoxicated students, documenting incidents.

After-dark exterior round of the building perimeter and grounds: parking lots and garages, courtyards, entrances and gates; look for unauthorized persons or loitering, lighting failures, unsecured exterior doors and hazards; report to campus security or on-call staff.

sources.transferJustification: Eldercare 'night shift patrol for resident ...' is the same work unit as a residential advisor's rounds: traversing a residential facility on a schedule, observing residents and premises, and alerting staff to problems.

sources.transferJustification: Vendor description of the same work unit: scheduled rounds of a residential facility checking residents' wellbeing and the premises, escalating problems to staff.

sources.transferJustification: Guard-tour rounds of corridors and common areas inside an institution-controlled building are the 'areas are safe and secure' half of this task: same routes, same objects (doors, leaks, hazards, unauthorized persons), same log-and-escalate output.

sources.transferJustification: Safety-check rounds of a residential care building (door status, fire equipment) are the premises-security portion of this task, carried out in the same class of facility.

sources.title: Autonomous Navigating Robot for Detecting Falls and Risk of Falls in Nursing Home Residents With Alzheimer Disease/ADRD - Feasibility Study (ClinicalTrials.gov NCT07451223)
sources.claim: A 2025 feasibility study tested an autonomously navigating robot that patrols nursing home rooms day and ... to detect falls, with nursing staff assessing the situation remotely through the robot's camera.
sources.transferJustification: In-room patrol checking residents' condition is the resident-safety half of rounds; the study shows it only at feasibility stage and with nurses making the assessment remotely, so it does not substantiate worker-quality timed watch checks.

tasks.label: Supervise students' housekeeping work to ensure that it is done properly.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: College residence-hall RA conducts scheduled health-and-safety room inspections of occupied student rooms: enters each room, checks for trash buildup, dirty dishes, spoiled food, blocked egress, bathroom/sink sanitation; judges against the housing standard, tells occupants what to remedy, logs findings and re-checks later. Rooms are personalized and cluttered, contents differ room to room.

Boarding-school dorm parent/houseparent performs daily morning room checks on students' rooms: beds made, floor and desk clear, trash emptied, laundry stowed; corrects students on the spot, requires re-doing before they leave for class, and reports repeat offenders. Time-boxed to a short window with students present.

Group-home or transitional-living staff assigns and supervises residents' chores in real time (kitchen cleanup after meals, bathroom scrubbing, vacuuming, taking out trash): demonstrates technique, watches the work, inspects the result, coaches residents with limited skills or behavioral issues, and requires re-doing until acceptable.

Post-chore inspection of shared institutional areas in a residence hall — communal kitchenette, lounge, hall bathroom, laundry room — after the resident chore rotation: verify surfaces wiped, floors swept, trash and recycling emptied, appliances cleaned; sign off the chore chart and notify the assigned residents who must redo work.

End-of-term / move-out cleaning inspection of vacated student rooms against a standard checklist: verify room cleaned to move-out standard (floor, closet, drawers, sink, refrigerator defrosted), photograph and document deficiencies, and assess cleaning charges or require the student to return and re-clean.

sources.title: Cobalt security robot to protect your people and places
sources.claim: Cobalt's indoor security robot autonomously runs scheduled and ad-hoc routes through offices and similar indoor facilities, performing patrols and facility checks and flagging anomalies (e.g., leaks, unexpected people) to a remote human specialist. This is the closest deployed analogue to walking rounds of a building, but it reports security/environmental events rather than judging whether assigned housekeeping was done properly or holding a resident accountable.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: autonomous indoor patrol/inspection rounds in a structured human work facility. It transfers only the locomotion-and-imaging portion of dorm rounds; it does not assess cleaning quality of arbitrary household surfaces, nor deliver the corrective supervision of a person that constitutes the task's accepted output.

sources.title: Boston Dynamics releases Spot and Orbit 5.1 with new Spot Cam - The Robot Report
sources.claim: Boston Dynamics Spot with Orbit runs autonomous inspection missions in industrial plants, capturing PTZ, thermal, acoustic and gauge readings on repeatable routes and automatically flagging anomalies against thresholds. Deployed in customer facilities (e.g., J-POWER).
sources.transferJustification: Related task: autonomous routine inspection with anomaly detection and reporting. Transfer is limited: the inspected items are fixed, pre-taught assets (gauges, motors, pipes) in an institution-controlled plant, not the varied, as-found contents of a lived-in student room, and no judgment of a person's work quality is produced.

sources.system: Autonomous cleaning-audit robot (audit sensor + exploration strategy)
sources.developer: Singapore University of Technology and Design (SUTD)
sources.title: An Autonomous Robot-Aided Auditing Scheme for Floor Cleaning (Sensors, MDPI)
sources.claim: A research mobile robot from SUTD audits floor-cleaning quality, using a 'touch and inspect' dust-sampling sensor plus vision to assign a cleanliness score for an area after cleaning. It is a laboratory/indoor test-area prototype limited to floor dust, not a fielded system that certifies whether a person's assigned housekeeping was done properly.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: robotic auditing of cleaning quality — the inspection core of this task. It does not transfer to the instances: it scores floor dust in a controlled test space only, is a prototype rather than a deployed system, and covers none of the room-contents assessment or resident follow-up.

tasks.label: Accompany and supervise students during meals.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Boarding/prep school: dorm faculty member accompanies assigned students to a required cafeteria or family-style seated meal in the school dining hall, takes attendance, sits at the table, enforces dress code and conduct, mediates disputes, prompts cleanup and releases students.

Youth group home (foster care / juvenile residential): staff eats with 6-10 residents around the kitchen table of a converted house, serves and portions food, enforces dietary and behavior plans, redirects and de-escalates arguments or food-related acting out, supervises chores after the meal.

Residential facility for people with intellectual/developmental disabilities: staff supervises a small dining room, provides hands-on assistance to some residents (cutting food, positioning, verbal prompts, aspiration and choking precautions), watches for medical events, and documents intake.

Residential treatment or behavioral-health program (e.g., eating disorder, substance use): staff runs a protocol-driven supervised meal - observing completion, blocking contraband or purging behaviors, coaching residents through distress, then providing post-meal supervision and charting.

College dorm or residential summer/bridge program: RA accompanies a group of students from the residence hall to the campus dining hall, does a headcount, sits with the group during the meal, handles conduct or roommate issues that surface, and walks them back.

Escort leg only: walking a group of residents along campus paths or public sidewalks between the residence and the dining facility in varied weather and traffic, keeping the group together and monitoring behavior en route.

sources.title: Florida School Deploys Knightscope Autonomous Security Robot (ASR)
sources.claim: Knightscope's K5 Autonomous Security Robot was deployed on a school campus, where it autonomously patrols and deters, detects and reports incidents; it does not supervise students, manage behavior, or physically intervene.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: security patrol/monitoring of a school campus, an E2 facility. It transfers only the passive presence-and-observation part of meal supervision; the robot reports to human officers and cannot enforce rules, mediate student conflict, take responsibility for minors, or act physically, so it cannot complete the instance.

sources.title: Cobalt security robot to protect your people and places
sources.claim: Cobalt's indoor security robot patrols human workplaces autonomously, but any interaction with a person is handled through two-way audio/video by a remote human specialist rather than by the robot itself.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: autonomous indoor monitoring of a structured human facility. It shows that in the closest commercially deployed analogue, person-facing judgment and interaction are escalated to remote humans, so the supervisory core of the meal task is not performed by the machine.

sources.title: Serve Robotics to Acquire Diligent Robotics, Expanding Physical AI Platform Beyond the Sidewalk
sources.claim: Moxi is an autonomous mobile robot deployed in more than 25 ..., but its work is fetching and delivering supplies, medications and lab samples - not supervising or accompanying people.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: autonomous navigation and errands inside a structured care facility (E2). It establishes that mobility among people in such settings is solved, but the delivered work is logistics; no capability for duty-of-care supervision, behavior management, or emergency intervention at a meal is demonstrated.

sources.title: Obi 3 Robotic Feeding Device – Adaptive Mealtime Independence IFD-500-031
sources.claim: The Obi robotic feeding device delivers bites to a single diner under the diner's own switch control, after a caregiver teaches bowl and delivery positions; it does not monitor a dining group or supervise a meal.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: hands-on mealtime assistance for a person who cannot self-feed, the physical-assistance element of the IDD instance. It does not transfer: the device is user-commanded rather than autonomous, is fixed to one place setting, and provides none of the group monitoring, safety judgment, or documentation the instance requires.

tasks.label: Provide transportation or escort for expeditions, such as shopping trips or visits to doctors or dentists.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Group home for adults with intellectual/developmental disabilities or serious mental illness: advisor drives one to three residents in the agency van to a doctor or dentist appointment on public roads, helps them in and out of the vehicle (walkers, seatbelts, occasional wheelchair securement), walks them into the office, sits in on the visit to relay history and receive instructions, stops at a pharmacy, and returns them home.

Residential care/group home shopping expedition: advisor drives two to four residents to a supermarket, Walmart or mall, supervises them inside the store, helps them choose items within a budget, assists at checkout with cash or benefit cards, loads bags into the van, and carries and puts away purchases at the residence.

Youth residential program (foster/treatment group home, boarding school, Job Corps center): advisor transports several adolescents in a facility van to medical, dental, court or activity appointments, maintaining headcount, managing behavior and conflicts en route, signing them in as the responsible adult, and remaining with them until return.

Independent, ambulatory resident (transitional/sober-living house, college dorm, senior residence): advisor simply provides the ride, dropping the resident at a clinic, dentist, pharmacy or store and picking them up afterward; no in-appointment support, physical assistance or in-store supervision is expected.

On-foot escort on institution-controlled premises: advisor walks or wheels a resident from the residence hall to an on-campus health center, counseling office or clinic across the facility's own walkways and corridors, mainly to get them there safely and on time.

sources.title: Waymo begins fully autonomous ops with 6th-gen Driver, targets 1M weekly rides | Electrek
sources.claim: Waymo runs fully driverless, paid, commercial robotaxi service on public roads in six US cities at roughly 400,000 paid rides per week, i.e. it can carry a passenger from a residence to a clinic or store and back without a human driver.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: point-to-point passenger transport on public roads. It transfers to the 'provide transportation' half of this task because the payload (a person), the road environment and the door-to-door itinerary are the same as a staff van trip to a clinic or store.

sources.title: Waymo teen accounts offer peace of mind for Phoenix families
sources.claim: Waymo permits linked teen accounts so riders aged 14-17 ride the driverless vehicle unaccompanied, showing the driverless ride can be used for a young rider travelling without an adult in the car.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: unaccompanied minor ride-hailing. It bears on transporting older adolescents from a residential program, though it provides no adult supervision, custody sign-in or behavior management during the trip.

sources.title: DTW adds Whill autonomous wheelchairs to McNamara Terminal | Crain's Detroit Business
sources.claim: WHILL's self-driving mobility chairs autonomously carry a passenger along mapped routes inside airport terminals (Winnipeg, Detroit, Anchorage), then return to base by themselves; over 100 units are deployed across US airports.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: conveying a person who needs help getting somewhere from one point to another inside an institution-controlled building. It transfers to a within-campus escort because the deliverable (person delivered to the appointment location safely and on time) and the controlled indoor setting match.

sources.title: Wheelchair-accessible vehicles - Waymo Help
sources.claim: Waymo cannot serve riders with mobility-related disabilities autonomously: its wheelchair-accessible vehicle rides are driven manually by human ..., so boarding assistance and securement for such riders is still a human job.

sources.system: IntBot humanoid 'José'; BotsAndUs guide robots; Aethon TUG
sources.title: US airport deploys humanoid robot to greet and help passengers
sources.claim: Airport and hospital service robots that interact with the public are limited to greeting, wayfinding, guiding and delivery functions; none supervise or physically assist a dependent person through an errand.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: public-facing assistance robots in a structured facility. Cited to bound what deployed service robots do — information and guidance only, no physical assistance, shopping help or custodial supervision.

tasks.label: Direct and participate in on- and off-campus recreational activities for residents of institutions, boarding schools, fraternities or sororities, children's homes, or similar establishments.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Residence-hall social/game night: the RA plans a floor program in the dorm lounge, hauls and sets up tables, snacks and board/video games, then plays and mingles with 10-30 college students for two hours, keeps the group engaged, handles noise/conflict issues, and cleans up.

Active recreation on campus grounds: RA organizes and physically plays in a pickup basketball/volleyball game, intramural match or outdoor field games with residents; carries out balls, nets and cones, sets teams, referees, participates athletically, and handles minor injuries.

Off-campus outing: RA drives or rides a van/bus with residents to a mall, movie theater, museum, pro game or amusement park; buys tickets, does head counts in crowds, supervises minors or students in public space, and responds to lost/ill/misbehaving participants.

Group home / children's home recreation: house parent leads an in-house craft, cooking, or active game session with 4-8 youth who may have behavioral or emotional needs; distributes materials, joins in, redirects and de-escalates behavior, ensures safety.

Outdoor adventure trip for boarding-school residents: day hike, camping, ropes course or ski trip; RA carries gear over rough terrain, sets up equipment, participates alongside students, and manages weather, fatigue and safety away from campus.

Structured seated group program in the facility common room: bingo, trivia night, movie discussion or a guided stretch/wellness session for residents seated at tables; RA sets out cards/prizes/materials, runs the session front-of-room, prompts participation, and closes it out.

sources.developer: University of Toronto Autonomous Systems and Biomechatronics Lab (G. Nejat)
sources.title: Robot-Delivered Cognitive Stimulation Games for Older Adults: Usability and Acceptability Evaluation
sources.claim: The socially assistive robot Tangy autonomously facilitated group bingo sessions for 18 older adults in a long-term care facility after being taught the game by caregivers - the closest demonstrated case of a robot running a group recreational activity for residents of an institution.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: facilitating a group game for residents of a residential institution, comparable to an RA's bingo/trivia night. Transfer is only partial - Tangy calls a seated game while staff distribute cards, recruit participants, set up and supervise, so it does not cover a whole RA program instance.

sources.developer: Trinity College Dublin / Akara Robotics (Conor McGinn)
sources.title: Robots rise to meet the challenge of caring for old people (Nature news feature)
sources.claim: The Stevie II service robot hosted bingo and sing-along sessions for residents at the Knollwood retirement community, with the activities director present throughout; the autonomy of its hosting is not established.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: front-of-room hosting of a recreational activity in a residential facility. Because autonomy during hosting is not established and staff remained in the room running the session, it cannot support a positive judgment.

sources.title: Outplaying elite table tennis players with an autonomous robot
sources.claim: Sony AI's Ace robot autonomously plays competitive table tennis against elite and professional human players on an instrumented laboratory rig - showing a machine can physically participate in one fixed recreational game, but not organize, supervise or join varied group sport.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: physically participating in a recreational game with a human. Transfer is limited: the system is a fixed-base arm on a purpose-built, densely instrumented table and does nothing to direct, set up, or supervise a residents' recreation program.

sources.title: Aging Japan: Robots May Have Role in Future of Elder Care (VOA)
sources.claim: Humanoid Pepper robots are used in Japanese elder-care facilities to lead group exercise routines for residents, with care staff present; the routines are pre-programmed content and independent autonomy is not established.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: leading a seated group activity in a residential institution. Autonomy is unclear and human staff run and supervise the session, so it cannot substantiate whole-instance completion of an RA-led program.

sources.system: social robots in classrooms (field-study review, incl. NAO, Pepper)
sources.title: The use of social robots in classrooms: A review of field-based studies
sources.claim: A review of field studies of social robots in schools finds robots are seldom run autonomously for more than a few days and that personalization and safety in real settings remain unsolved - evidence against sustained autonomous robot-led programming with children and adolescents.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: autonomous robot engagement with groups of young people in an institutional setting; the review documents that such deployments remain short, supervised research trials rather than worker-quality substitutes.

tasks.label: Sort and distribute mail.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Residence-hall / campus mail center: a residential advisor or mail-center staffer receives the day's tray of letters, flats, magazines and small parcels addressed to hundreds of students, matches each name against the current room/box roster, and drops each piece into the correct pigeonhole mailbox in a wall of boxes.

Front desk / package room of a dorm or group facility: carrier drops a cart of parcels; the advisor scans or logs each one, shelves it by resident, sends a pickup notice, then retrieves it and hands it over after checking the resident's ID, recording the pickup.

Group home / small residential facility (6-12 residents): the advisor collects the day's mail from the curbside box, sorts the small mixed stack by resident name (screening for mail to former residents or for facility business), then walks it to each resident's room or personal cubby, sometimes handing it directly to the resident amid ordinary household clutter and furniture.

Exception handling at the mail station: pieces addressed to residents who moved out, graduated or were never assigned there; mis-addressed pieces; mail to be held for absent residents or forwarded; certified/accountable items needing a signature log; return-to-sender marking and re-dispatch.

Door-to-door distribution along dorm/facility corridors: the advisor carries pre-sorted bundles of mail, flyers and notices on a round through corridors and floors, leaving each item at or under the resident's door or handing it to the resident who answers.

sources.date: 2026-06 (product page last modified); product line marketed since ~2015
sources.title: Mail Matrix: Automated Mail Sorting System | OPEX
sources.claim: OPEX Mail Matrix is a commercial automated mail-sorting machine whose wireless iBOT robots sort mixed envelopes, flats, magazines and small parcels ... as many as 1,020 delivery bins in a single ..., with MLOCR address reading and ODBC lookup against an external recipient database.

sources.system: OPEX Mail Matrix at Liberty University Postal Services
sources.title: OPEX Mail Matrix Automates The Mailroom At Liberty University
sources.claim: Liberty University installed the Mail ... in its campus mail center to sort inbound mail to students and staff; the operator loads mail into the feeder and the iBOTs sort each piece to the correct recipient location, eliminating manual name look-ups and ~126 hours of semester-start overtime.
sources.transferJustification: Same task: sorting inbound student mail by recipient in a campus/residential mail operation, the work a residential advisor does at a dorm mailroom.

sources.title: Relay Delivery Robots – Leader in delivery robots for hospitals and hotels
sources.claim: Relay delivery robots autonomously carry packages, amenities and room-service items through hotel corridors to individual guest rooms, navigating hallways, security doors and elevators without human control; the fleet reports over 1,000,000 lifetime deliveries at a 99.8% success rate.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: item delivery to occupied rooms along institutional corridors. Objects (envelopes, small parcels), corridor/elevator environment and recipient hand-off match door-to-door mail distribution in a dormitory.

sources.title: Relay Robotics – Providing autonomous service robots that work with humans safely, securely, reliably, and contact-free
sources.claim: Relay robots are deployed at major US hotel chains and hospitals, indicating a fielded rather than experimental system for corridor and guest-room delivery.
sources.transferJustification: Same transfer as above: fielded autonomous indoor delivery to individual rooms in institution-controlled buildings.

sources.date: 2026-07 (product page retrieved); product in service since ~2017 (Edison Award 2017)
sources.title: Cleveron 402 - Cleveron
sources.claim: Cleveron 402 is a commercially deployed robotic parcel locker that accepts parcels inserted at a console, measures and stores each one on internal shelves under machine control, rearranges stock while idle, and dispenses a parcel to the correct authenticated recipient in about 10 seconds; installed by retailers including Zara/Inditex, Asda, Decathlon and Falabella.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: parcel intake, tracked storage and authenticated hand-out to a named recipient — the same operation as a residence-hall package room, with the same objects (parcels up to locker size).

sources.system: Postal Automated Redirection System (PARS) on USPS letter sorting equipment
sources.title: Postal Automated Redirection System | Office of Inspector General OIG
sources.claim: USPS Postal Automated Redirection System, deployed in 2007, uses mail-sorting equipment to automatically intercept letter mail that is undeliverable as addressed, match it to a change-of-address record, apply the new address and re-sort it for forwarding.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: machine identification and physical diversion/relabeling of mail addressed to people no longer at the address — the same exception handling (former residents, forwarding, return-to-sender) an advisor performs on dorm mail.

sources.system: Figure 02 humanoid with Helix vision-language-action policy
sources.date: 2025-09 (hour-long autonomous sorting footage); Helix logistics update 2025-06
sources.title: Figure’s Autonomous Robot Is Able To Sort All Types Of Packages And They Just Posted An Hour Of Uninterrupted Footage To Prove It
sources.claim: Figure 02 humanoids running the Helix policy autonomously sort mixed shipping items — rigid boxes, poly-bagged parcels and flat envelopes — onto conveyors in a logistics sorting facility, shown in hour-long uninterrupted footage.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: singulating and sorting mixed mail-class objects (envelopes, bags, boxes) presented on a conveyor — the manipulation core of mail/parcel sorting, but only demonstrated in a purpose-built conveyor cell.

tasks.label: Inventory, pack, and remove items left behind by former residents.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: End-of-term college residence hall cleanout: after checkout, the RA/hall director walks a standard double room, separates trash from keepable property (clothing, bedding, textbooks, chargers, toiletries, shoes, food), writes an itemized abandoned-property list, bags/boxes the items, labels each box with the former resident's name and room, and carries or carts them to the building's storage room.

Group home / residential treatment or recovery facility: a resident is discharged, absconds, or is removed; staff itemize belongings (clothing, toiletries, medications, ID documents, phone, cash/valuables) on a signed and witnessed personal-property inventory form, bag or box them, and secure them in a locked storage area pending pickup, per licensing policy.

Boarding school or college mid-term departure: a student withdraws or is removed and does not return; staff pack the entire contents of the room (closet, drawers, desk, under-bed bins) into cartons, record contents, tape and label the boxes, and stage them for family pickup or carrier shipment.

Shelter / transitional housing bed turnover: belongings left at a bed, locker, or cubby by a departed resident are logged on a property log, bagged, tagged with date and name, and moved to a storage cage; soiled bedding, perishables, and hazardous items are discarded and noted.

Scattered-site supportive housing apartment or house-style group home after a resident moves out or is evicted: a whole dwelling of leftover possessions, sometimes cluttered or hoarded, with mixed trash, food waste, furniture, and personal papers; staff inventory, pack, and clear it so the unit can be re-let.

Bulky leftovers at any of these facilities: mini-fridge, microwave, futon or papasan chair, TV, suitcases, sports equipment, rolled rugs; staff log them, wrap or strap them, and haul them down corridors/elevators to a storage cage, dumpster, or donation pickup.

sources.title: Amazon's Sparrow is leaving the nest: Trailblazing warehouse robot is ready for a wider rollout – GeekWire
sources.claim: Amazon's Sparrow autonomously picks and moves individual, diverse products from cluttered totes in deployed fulfillment centers, identifying items with computer vision before placing them in another container.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: piece-picking of heterogeneous consumer goods. The objects (clothing in polybags, books, toiletries, small electronics) are the same classes of items left behind by residents, and the system both recognizes and singulates them, which is the core of inventorying and packing when items are presented to the machine.

sources.title: Amazon Testing Robotic Arm that Identifies Individual Products | Vision Systems Design
sources.claim: Sparrow handles a very large fraction of a heterogeneous item catalog and both picks from cluttered totes and packs items densely into another bin.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: tote-to-tote item handling. Demonstrates identification plus placement of unknown-to-the-cell items into a receptacle, i.e., the pack step when items are presented on a line; the excluded class (large appliances) is handled by other cited systems.

sources.system: OSARO AutoModel piece-picking / robotic bagging system
sources.title: OSARO's AI-Driven Automation Enhances Fulfillment Speed and Accuracy | RoboticsTomorrow
sources.claim: OSARO's piece-picking robots identify, pick, and place individual e-commerce items into bags for sealing and shipping, deployed at a large e-commerce fulfillment operation.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: robotic bagging of individual goods. Packing left-behind clothing and small personal effects into labeled bags/boxes at a station is the same pick-identify-place-into-container-and-seal cycle, with comparable object types and precision.

sources.title: AMP's Horowitz on Bringing AI to the Recycling World | Waste360
sources.claim: AMP's Cortex robots classify and pick heterogeneous, previously unseen mixed-stream objects off a moving conveyor at high accuracy in operating recycling facilities.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: mixed-stream waste sortation. Abandoned-property processing is dominated by unlabeled, novel, mixed objects that must be categorized (keep vs. discard, item type) and placed in the right receptacle, which is exactly what Cortex does at production reliability when material is presented on a line.

sources.title: Heavy Picker | Sorting Robot | ZenRobotics
sources.claim: ZenRobotics Heavy Picker autonomously grips and sorts bulky, heavy, irregular objects (up to about 30 kg) on waste sorting lines, running unattended around the clock.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: bulky waste sortation. Mini-fridges, rolled rugs, suitcases and futon parts fall in the same size/weight/irregularity class as bulky C&D and municipal waste objects that the Heavy Picker grips and redirects when presented on a sorting line.

sources.title: From case unloading to picking and beyond with DHL and Boston Dynamics - Automated Warehouse
sources.claim: Boston Dynamics' Stretch autonomously unloads and moves cases in logistics facilities and is deployed commercially by DHL at scale.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: autonomous case handling. The 'remove' step — moving sealed, labeled cartons of belongings off the line into storage or onto a pallet/truck — is the same box-handling operation at the same weights and reliability.

sources.title: Figure Humanoid Robots Sort Packages Non-Stop in 24/7 Demo | TechRepublic
sources.claim: Figure's Helix-02 humanoids sorted tens of thousands of parcels of varied size and packaging fully autonomously over a multi-day livestreamed run at a customer warehouse.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: parcel singulation and sortation at a conveyor station. Shows sustained, uninterrupted autonomous handling of varied deformable and rigid packages at a fixtured station, supporting the pack/stage step when belongings are presented to the machine.

sources.title: Two Autonomous Humanoid Robots Seamlessly Work Together to Make the Bed | Laughing Squid
sources.claim: The most advanced room-level tidying by a humanoid is a short staged demonstration: two Helix-02 robots autonomously put items away, took out trash, and made a bed in a staged bedroom in about two minutes.
sources.transferJustification: Directly related: in-room object pickup. It is cited to show the current ceiling in real rooms is a brief staged demo without itemized documentation, boxing, labeling, or hauling, so it does not establish worker-quality completion inside a residence hall.

sources.title: A VLA with Open-World Generalization (π0.5)
sources.claim: Physical Intelligence's pi-0.5 robot can clean bedrooms and kitchens in homes not seen in training, but the developers state it is far from perfect ... frequently makes mistakes.
sources.transferJustification: Directly related: picking up and putting away arbitrary household objects in unseen dwellings. Cited to show that unstructured-dwelling clearing remains research-grade and error-prone, below the reliability an employer would accept for an abandoned-property inventory.

sources.title: TidyBot: personalized robot assistance with large language models | Autonomous Robots
sources.claim: TidyBot, a research mobile manipulator, put away 85% of objects in real-world household cleanup tests.
sources.transferJustification: Directly related: autonomous in-room pickup of scattered personal objects. An 85% put-away rate in curated test rooms is well short of the near-complete, itemized clearing an employer requires, supporting the negative judgment at E2/E3.

Small-format store (convenience store, boutique, jewelry counter, mall kiosk, pharmacy front end): tight aisles, goods in drawers, showcases, coolers and under-counter bins; the supervisor eyeballs/counts stock and reorders through the POS or a vendor rep.

Trade-in, customer-return and buyback merchandise examined at the service counter or backroom: phones/electronics, games, tools or returned goods are inspected for damage, completeness and function and graded for restock, markdown, refurbishment or return-to-vendor.

tasks.label: Examine merchandise to ensure correct pricing and display, and that it functions as advertised.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Wholesale club / cash-and-carry or distributor showroom floor walk before opening: the supervisor goes down aisles and pallet racks checking that shelf price labels and promo signage match the current price file, that items sit in their planogrammed slots with correct facings and display set-ups, and flags mislabeled, misplaced, damaged or expired packaged goods on standard steel shelving.

Distribution warehouse staging area: the supervisor spot-checks pallets and cases staged for customer orders or a promotion - case/SKU labels, quantities, lot and expiry codes, and the pricing paperwork applied - against the order and system records before release to the customer or route truck.

Branch counter operation (parts, electrical, industrial supply, electronics wholesaler): the supervisor pulls the specific item a rep quoted or a customer questioned, confirms the model/spec matches the advertised description and the quoted price, powers it up or bench-tests it, and accepts or rejects the unit before it ships.

Vehicle, RV or heavy-equipment dealership lot: the supervisor walks the display line, checks window-sticker/price display and staging of each unit, starts the unit, and verifies that advertised options and features actually work; outdoor lot, mixed weather, customers and porters moving through.

Route/DSD or manufacturer-rep display audit inside a customer's store or branch: the supervisor verifies the contracted products, price points, promo signage and end-cap/display arrangement are as sold, and that stock on display is fresh and undamaged.

Demo and sample units checked at the branch showroom or before a trade show: the supervisor powers on demo equipment (electronics, appliances, instruments, tools), confirms the advertised functions perform, and checks that current price sheets/labels are attached to each sample.

instances.label: Supermarket or big-box staffed checkout lane: cashier totals the order on the POS, prompts the customer to dip/tap/swipe a credit, debit or mobile wallet at the pin-pad, watches for approval or decline, handles re-tries, prints and hands over the receipt. Indoor, fixed lane, high volume.

Supermarket, discount or general-merchandise staffed lane: customer tenders cash. Cashier scans paper/manufacturer coupons first, keys the tender, accepts bills and coins, counts change out of the drawer, returns change plus receipt, keeps the drawer balanced.

Quick-service restaurant, coffee shop or cafeteria front counter: rapid-fire small-ticket transactions, mixed cash and card, gift cards and tip prompts, change handed back within seconds during a rush.

Drive-thru window: cashier leans out of a window to take a card or cash from a driver in a vehicle, runs the tender, returns change, receipt and the card, under strict service-time targets and in outdoor weather at the window.

Convenience store, gas station or pharmacy counter: cash and cards plus EBT/SNAP tender, split tenders, lottery voucher/credit redemption, prepaid and gift card activation, fuel prepay reconciliation.

Exception tenders anywhere in retail: personal check with ID capture and verification, paper WIC/manufacturer rebate vouchers requiring adjudication, house-account or store-credit charges, manager-approved manual overrides.

instances.label: Supermarket/big-box front-end lead works the lane row during a shift: watches queue build-up and lane coverage, pages backup cashiers, opens and closes lanes, sends cashiers to breaks and pulls them back. tasks.label: Establish or identify prices of goods, services, or admission, and tabulate bills, using calculators, cash registers, or optical price scanners.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Supermarket / big-box checkout lane: customer unloads a cart of 20-60 mixed goods onto a belt; cashier grabs each item, orients and passes the barcode over the scanner, weighs and keys PLUs for loose produce, handles bulky/awkward items (cases of water, bagged pet food), keys prices for unbarcoded or damaged-label items, applies coupons and price overrides, and produces a correct running total in a few minutes.

Convenience store, gas station, drugstore or liquor store front counter: small baskets of 1-8 items, many barcoded but some priced by hand (bakery, deli, hot food, single cigarettes/lottery), fuel pump amounts read from the console, occasional manual price entry from a posted list, all while the queue moves quickly.

Quick-service restaurant, cafeteria or stadium/concession counter: worker hears or sees the customer's order (or the items on a tray), enters items, combos, sizes and modifiers into the POS touchscreen, applies menu prices and promos, and reads back the total.

Department, apparel, hardware or specialty store register: tagged merchandise placed on the counter, some tags missing or marked down, cashier scans or keys SKUs, performs price lookups/price checks for customers (including walking the item to a scanner or checking shelf tags), applies discounts and totals the sale.

Admission / service-fee booth: cinema, museum, attraction, pool or parking cashier determines the applicable rate (adult/child/senior, matinee, member, hours parked), tabulates the amount owed and issues a ticket or receipt.

Mobile or outdoor vending: farmers market stall, food truck, fair or festival booth, sidewalk sale; goods are loose or weighed, prices come from a handwritten sign or the vendor's head, and the bill is tallied on a calculator or phone-based card reader in wind, sun and crowds.

tasks.label: Process merchandise returns and exchanges.

instances.label: Big-box/department store customer service desk: customer presents a general-merchandise item (small appliance, toy, apparel, opened electronics box) with receipt; cashier verifies the item matches the receipt, checks condition/completeness/tags/accessories, applies return policy, issues a card or cash refund, and routes the item to restock, defect, or salvage bin.

Grocery/drugstore front-end register: quick return or swap of a small item (wrong or spoiled product, damaged package, unwanted item), scanned and refunded in cash from the till, item set aside for restock or spoilage; done between ordinary checkout customers.

Contested return: no receipt, worn/used/damaged goods, past the return window, missing parts, or suspected return fraud; cashier inspects, negotiates with the customer, scans ID into the return-authorization system, issues store credit or denies the return, and calls a manager for override.

Exchange: customer swaps size, color, or a defective unit; cashier verifies the returned item, checks or fetches the replacement from the sales floor, reconciles any price difference, processes the even-exchange transaction, and bags the replacement.

In-store drop-off of an online-order return (BORIS/carrier returns desk): customer presents a QR code or packing slip with a boxed or bagged item; worker scans the code, accepts the item into store custody without opening it, triggers the refund, and consolidates it into a returns bin or bag.

Bottle/can deposit redemption at a supermarket front end in a bottle-bill state: customer returns beverage containers, which must be identified as eligible, counted, sorted, and the deposit refunded as cash, voucher, or store credit.

instances.label: Supermarket or big-box cashier ends a shift: carries the till to the store's cash office, counts bills and coins, runs the POS tender/sales report for the shift, records over/short and prepares the deposit. Indoor, institution-controlled store back office.

Convenience store or gas station clerk at shift change: runs an X/Z register report, counts the drawer, drops excess bills into the safe, and reconciles counted cash plus card batch totals against shift sales; high tender mix, frequent interruptions.

Quick-service restaurant or coffee shop cashier at close: counts the drawer against the POS station report, batches the card terminal, accounts for tips and paid-outs, and reports the shift's cash over/short to the manager.

Small independent retailer, boutique, pharmacy counter or hardware store: single register closed out at end of day; count currency and coin, tally checks, coupons, gift certificates and manual slips, compare with register tape/POS totals, prepare bank deposit.

Mobile or event cashier (farmers-market stall, food truck, fair or festival concession): counts a cash box at end of the day outdoors against a tablet POS or handwritten sales tally, no fixed facility or standard layout.

tasks.label: Count money in cash drawers at the beginning of shifts to ensure that amounts are correct and that there is adequate change.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Supermarket/big-box grocery cashier starting a shift: picks up an assigned till from the cash office or safe, counts the bills and coin rolls (typically a $100-$200 float) against the assigned amount, checks that enough $1s, $5s and coin are present, signs the till log and reports any discrepancy before opening the lane.

Convenience store / gas station clerk at shift change: counts the drawer at the front counter with the outgoing clerk, mostly small bills and coin, while customers may walk up; verifies against the POS-recorded starting bank and adds change from the safe if short.

Quick-service restaurant, coffee shop or cafeteria cashier: manager issues a small starting bank (rolls of coin and small bills); the cashier counts it into the drawer at the register or in the office, verifies the total and confirms adequate change before the meal rush.

Specialty retail, pharmacy or department-store cashier: counts the register drawer at the register at the start of shift, verifies the float against the POS opening amount, checks denomination mix and requests coin rolls or small bills from the cash office if short.

High-volume cash venue (casino cage, stadium/cinema box office or concession): cashier draws a large impress bank, counts it under dual-verification rules with strapped bills and coin, and confirms denomination levels are adequate for expected payouts before the shift opens.

Mobile or temporary vendor cashier (food truck, farmers-market stall, festival or fair concession): counts the starting cash box on site, in the open air with no fixed premises, verifying float and change before serving.

instances.label: Supermarket/supercenter staffed checkout lane: at the end of an order the customer hands over a small stack of paper manufacturer and store coupons; the cashier scans each barcode, checks expiration and item match, resolves any that fail to scan, applies the discounts and drops the coupons in the till/coupon bin.

Issuing offers/rewards at the register: after the transaction the register's in-lane printer produces targeted 'checkout' coupons, loyalty reward certificates or promotional receipts tied to the shopper's card, which are printed, torn off and given to the customer (modern equivalent of issuing trading stamps).

Convenience store, drugstore or quick-service counter: single paper coupon or promotional voucher presented with a small purchase, plus SNAP EBT tender for eligible cold/packaged food; one register, small counter, cashier also bags and makes change.

Cashier staffing a bank of self-checkouts: intervening on exceptions - a paper coupon the machine rejects, an EBT card declined or a mixed-tender split the shopper cannot complete, judging whether the coupon is valid and overriding or refusing it.

Farmers market stand, mobile vendor or very small independent store: redeeming paper WIC/Farmers Market Nutrition Program vouchers or paper coupons that require manual price entry, checking the printed food list and signature, outdoors or on a folding-table register with no standard equipment.

instances.label: Supermarket/grocery checkout lane: cashier lifts loose produce (bananas, tomatoes, grapes in a bag, apples) off the moving belt or out of a cart, sets it on the integrated register scale, identifies the item and keys or looks up the PLU, and the POS multiplies weight by unit price; done at pace with a customer line, sometimes with tare for the produce bag.

Service counter (deli, meat, seafood, cheese, bakery): worker cuts/scoops product to the customer's requested amount, places it in a wrapper or tub on the counter scale, selects the product key, and the scale prints a weight/price label applied to the package.

Self-serve bulk section, candy, coffee, salad/hot bar: customer-filled bag or clamshell brought to the register or scale station; worker tares the container, weighs it, selects the correct bulk code, and prices the fill.

Farmers market, roadside stand, or outdoor vendor booth: vendor/cashier weighs loose produce in a bag or basket on a portable, hanging, or battery scale on an uneven table outdoors, computes price mentally or on a scale display, and collects payment.

Hardware store, garden center, nursery, or feed store: worker weighs loose fasteners, chain cut to length, seed, soil amendment, or animal feed on a floor or counter scale (often weigh-count for small parts) and prices the lot.

tasks.label: Sort, count, and wrap currency and coins.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: End-of-shift till count in a supermarket/big-box cash office: cashier carries the drawer in, pulls out checks/coupons/vouchers, stacks and faces mixed bills by denomination, counts loose coin from the drawer compartments, reconciles the total to the POS report, bands surplus bills and records the count.

Bulk deposit preparation in a cash-intensive store (grocery, convenience chain, amusement venue): several thousand loose coins accumulated from lanes are sorted by denomination and rolled into standard bank wrappers, bills are counted and put into $100 straps, deposit slip completed and cash sealed in a bank bag for the armored carrier.

Start-of-day float/change-order preparation in the cash office: breaking open coin rolls, counting out standard $100-$200 starting banks of mixed bills and coin into each register till, and verifying the change order received from the bank.

Mid-shift count or cash drop at the register on the sales floor with customers nearby: cashier counts the drawer or removes large bills, verifies a total quickly between transactions, and drops the counted cash into a drop safe.

Small independent shop, restaurant or coffee bar with no cash office: end-of-day count of a small, mixed, often crumpled bundle of bills plus coin and tips, done at the counter or a cluttered back-room desk with no dedicated cash equipment.

Mobile or outdoor vending: food truck, farmers-market stall, fair/festival concession or parking attendant counting and sorting the day's takings in a cramped, non-standard, sometimes windy or dim outdoor setting.

tasks.label: Keep periodic balance sheets of amounts and numbers of transactions.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Supermarket or big-box store, end of shift: the cashier's drawer is taken to the cash office, bills and coin are counted, totals are matched against the register's X/Z report (sales amount, tender split, number of transactions), and the figures plus over/short are entered on the daily balance sheet.

Convenience store, gas station, pharmacy or small specialty retailer, shift change at the counter: print the register report, count the drawer, record cash, card and transaction-count totals on the shift report/log, drop excess cash into the safe. Customers may be present throughout.

Restaurant, fast-food or coffee shop: cashier or shift lead reconciles the assigned bank at shift change in a back room, recording cash counted, card batch totals, transaction counts, paid-outs and over/short on shift paperwork, under time pressure between rushes.

Head cashier / cash-office periodic roll-up (daily to weekly): consolidating several tills and the safe into a periodic balance summary of amounts and numbers of transactions, plus deposit records; includes a residue of paper tender such as checks and coupons.

Card-dominant setting (box office, campus store, ticket or service kiosk): the periodic balance is chiefly running and logging POS/terminal batch reports of amounts and transaction counts, with a small cash float verified and recorded.

Mobile or outdoor cashiering: festival or farmers-market booth, food truck, parking attendant, seasonal stand. The cash box is counted and a tally sheet completed on a folding table or in a vehicle, in a setting no institution keeps to a standard.

Cart retrieval: going out into the store parking lot in all weather to collect shopping carts from corrals and stray spots, nesting a line of 10-25 carts and pushing them back to the vestibule through vehicle traffic.

Carry-out service: loading a customer's bagged groceries, bulk items (softener salt, mulch, feed, cases of water, a boxed TV) onto a cart, escorting the customer across the lot, and lifting the items into the trunk, back seat, or truck bed of their vehicle.

instances.label: Supermarket / big-box store: between customers or during slow periods the cashier works a cart or pallet of mixed cases out to the sales floor, cuts cases open, and fills aisle shelves and endcaps with assorted packaged goods (cans, boxes, bagged goods, bottles), placing them per planogram, facing/rotating stock, and breaking down cardboard, all while shoppers move through the aisle.

Convenience store / grocery: cashier keeps the customer-facing beverage cooler shelves filled, taking bottles and cans out of delivery crates staged in the walk-in cooler or behind the reach-in doors and loading them onto the cooler shelves, front-facing and rotating by date, repeatedly through the shift.

Small-format store (convenience, drug, gas station): restocking front-end and impulse displays near the register — candy racks, gum, snack pegs, magazines, tobacco/backbar cigarette fixtures, single-serve drinks — from small backroom cartons, in a cramped area behind and beside the checkstand.

Go-backs / returns: cashier takes a bin or cart of items abandoned at the checkout or handed back by customers (mixed groceries including chilled and frozen, apparel on hangers, small hardware, toys, cosmetics), identifies each item's home location, walks it across the sales floor and re-shelves or re-hangs it neatly in the correct spot.

Marking prices on individual items: applying price or markdown stickers with a hand price gun or printed label batches to packages and odd-shaped merchandise, sometimes removing or covering an old label, done at a backroom bench or on the floor at a clearance rack.

Marking prices on shelves: printing a batch of shelf-edge tags for price changes and sale events and swapping them into the correct label holders on the shelf rails throughout assigned aisles, plus hanging sale signage and clip strips.

instances.label: Supermarket checkout: cashier bags a 20-50 item grocery order arriving on a belt — cans, produce, eggs, bread, bottles, frozen and chilled items, chemicals — into plastic, paper or customer-supplied reusable bags, ordering by weight/fragility and keeping raw meat and chemicals separate, while the customer waits and often reaches into the bagging area.

Convenience store, pharmacy, dollar or general-merchandise register: cashier drops a handful of small packaged items (drinks, snacks, cosmetics, apparel) into a plastic or paper bag, sometimes double-bagging or attaching a receipt, at high speed with the customer at the counter.

Jackpot / hand-pay payoff: worker verifies the jackpot slip and patron ID, obtains the customer's signature on the receipt and W-2G tax paperwork, and disburses the cash at the booth or cage window.

Large or non-standard exchanges: redemptions above the jurisdictional kiosk/ticket limit requiring photo ID and Title 31 logging, credit markers and check cashing, foreign currency, damaged/discontinued chips or torn tickets, and disputed or miscounted transactions requiring supervisor involvement.

Bulk counting in the count room/vault: soft count of drop-box currency and tickets or hard count of coin buckets, done by a count team under surveillance, with contents emptied onto a count table, run through machines, verified and reconciled to meter/expected figures.
Counting and auditing the chip/token portion of a booth or cage bank: verifying racks of value chips and tokens by denomination against the inventory sheet at shift change or during a spot audit.

tasks.label: Reconcile daily summaries of transactions to balance books.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Slot booth / change booth cashier at end of shift: obtains the system-generated shift transaction summary (ticket redemptions, jackpot payouts, fills, chip and cash exchanges), compares it against the recorded opening and closing bank figures, computes the over/short, records the figures on the cash summary form, signs it and turns it in to the cage supervisor.

Main cage / main bank cashier performing the daily accountability reconciliation: totals cash, chips, TITO tickets, markers, fills/credits and kiosk transfers across the shift, reconciles the beginning inventory plus documented transactions to the closing balance in the cage accountability system, and forwards the signed reconciliation paperwork to accounting.

Change person reconciling a personal pouch/bank at shift end: matching the issued bank slip, pouch-pay receipts and hopper/ticket vouchers against the amount returned, and logging the result on the bank check-in record with a cage cashier.

Reconciling ancillary devices and windows: redemption kiosk, ATM/cash-advance, and check-cashing reports reconciled to system transaction logs and to the recorded canister/inventory figures, with the resulting variance entered on the daily summary.

Variance / discrepancy resolution: when the daily summary does not balance, researching individual transactions in the cage system, pulling receipts and signed payout slips, requesting surveillance review, correcting entries, and preparing a written variance report for accounting and regulators.

tasks.label: Obtain customers' signatures on receipts when winnings exceed the amount held in a slot machine.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Routine reportable hand pay on the main slot floor: a machine locks up on a $1,200–$5,000 win, the change person/slot attendant walks to the seated patron, verifies the lockup, inspects the patron's government photo ID and player card, presents the printed jackpot slip/W-2G and a pen, obtains the signature, hands the patron their copy, and retains the signed original. Crowded, noisy floor; patron may be at any of thousands of machines.

Sub-threshold hand pay (credit meter or hopper limit exceeded, no tax form required): attendant responds to the locked machine, prints or carries a payout receipt, has the seated patron sign it, and files the copy. Quick, low-documentation transaction at the patron's machine.

Booth/cage transaction: patron carries a jackpot slip, oversized TITO ticket, or payout voucher to the slot booth or cashier cage window; the cashier verifies the document against the system, checks ID where required, has the patron sign the payout receipt across the counter, and pays.

Large or complex jackpot: win of roughly $10,000+ or one requiring federal withholding, several co-winners each needing forms and signatures, Title 31/CTR paperwork, aggregated W-2Gs, name/ID discrepancies, or payment by check in a high-limit salon with a supervisor and security present.

Exception cases: disputed or malfunction-flagged jackpot, patron without acceptable ID, patron on a self-exclusion or banned list, underage or intoxicated patron, or a language barrier — verification, supervisor involvement, or refusal precedes any signature.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Cage cashier at a casino window: a patron presents a mixed pile or racks of chips to cash out; the cashier determines the denominations present and computes the total dollar value owed, announcing/entering the figure before the cash exchange.

Large or high-denomination cash-out: cashier computes the total value of a multi-denomination stack including $500/$1,000/$5,000 chips, cross-checks the figure against CTR/MTL thresholds and paperwork, and records the computed amount.
Slot-area booth cashier / change person computing the value of a patron's chips, tokens, or ticket vouchers for a payout, and figuring the correct change or payoff amount.
Shift-end drawer/bank audit: cashier tallies the chip inventory in the impressed bank by denomination and computes the total chip value to reconcile the bank to its accountability figure.

Table-area or poker-room related computation: cashier or booth attendant figures a player's net win/loss in chip value for a buy-in/cash-out, marker payoff, or jackpot verification, often keying figures into the casino management terminal.

tasks.label: Furnish change persons with a money bank at the start of each shift.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Large casino, slot-area booth or main cage window at shift change: the booth cashier pulls the standard imprest bank (e.g., $500–$2,000 in mixed currency denominations) for an arriving change person, counts it out at the window, has the change person count it back, and both sign the bank/imprest slip before the change person takes the tray or bag to the floor.

Cage/vault bank preparation ahead of a shift: cashier makes up several employee banks in advance (specified denomination mixes counted into drawers, trays or locked bags), verifies each under dual control, logs them, and issues them across the window as change persons clock in.

Bank that includes coin: cashier counts out loose coin and/or rolled coin along with small bills for a change person who will break bills and feed coin-taking machines, verifies the coin amount, and records it on the bank slip.

Small property (card room, bingo hall, small tribal casino, racino) with one booth: cashier manually counts a bank out of the booth safe or drawer, sometimes in a non-standard amount or with a special denomination request from the change person, hands it over and gets a signature in a paper log.

Bank furnished away from the main booth: cashier carries or escorts banks out to a satellite booth, kiosk area, or to a change person on the floor mid-shift (supplemental bank, bank bag and key handover), verifying and signing at the point of delivery.

tasks.label: Listen for jackpot alarm bells and issue payoffs to winners.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Taxable hand-pay on a busy slot floor: machine locks up with candle light/alarm at a $1,200+ (now inflation-adjusted) jackpot; attendant walks to the machine, verifies the win against the slot system, collects the patron's photo ID and SSN, prepares and prints the W-2G, counts out the cash at the machine and obtains a signature, then clears the lockup.

Non-taxable hand pay / short pay / hopper-type lockup: attendant responds to the alarm, confirms the amount on the slot system, pays a few hundred dollars in cash from a pouch or bank at the machine, logs the payout and resets the game. No tax paperwork; speed matters.

Booth or cage-window payoff: patron brings a jackpot slip, hand-pay voucher or TITO ticket to the slot booth/cage; the booth cashier validates it against the slot accounting system, counts out currency through the window, obtains the signature and files the paperwork, working from a fixed till and bank.

Large progressive/top-award jackpot (tens of thousands of dollars or more): the machine locks up, a slot technician and supervisor verify the game and meters, surveillance signs off, management approves, photos and extended paperwork are done, and payment is made in bulk cash or by check, often with two verifiers.

Route / limited-gaming venue (tavern, truck stop, fraternal club, small satellite gaming room): a machine alarms with a win; the single on-duty attendant or bartender verifies the ticket/meter, pays the winner from a small cash bank behind the bar and records the payout.

tasks.label: Sell gambling chips, tokens, or tickets to patrons, or to other workers for resale to patrons.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Casino cage/booth window, routine chip buy-in: patron slides $20-$1,000 in cash (or a TITO voucher) under the glass; cashier verifies notes for counterfeits, counts out table-game chips of the requested denominations, pushes them through the window and logs the transaction.

Casino cage, high-value or complex chip sale: buy-ins over the CTR/Title 31 threshold requiring ID capture and multiple-transaction logging, chips issued against a signed marker/credit line, foreign currency or check buy-ins, non-negotiable promotional chips, and color-ups where the cashier verifies signatures and exercises judgment.

Slot-area change booth or roving change person: patron hands over bills and receives coin/tokens, broken bills, or a cash-equivalent gaming ticket/voucher to play with; high volume, small amounts, on the open gaming floor.

Race and sports book ticket window: patron states a wager verbally or on a bet slip; writer keys it into the tote/sportsbook terminal, takes the cash, prints the wager ticket and hands it over, under peak-event time pressure.

Keno, bingo, pull-tab and lottery counter (casino lounge, bingo hall, or lottery/OTB retail counter): selling keno tickets, bingo paper packs or electronic units, pull-tabs and lottery tickets to patrons for cash.

Selling/issuing to other workers rather than patrons: furnishing change persons with imprest money banks at shift start, issuing coin rolls or ticket/paper inventory to floor sellers, and dispensing chip fills from the cage for table trays, with counts, paperwork and signatures.

tasks.label: Clean casino areas.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: On a live slot floor, the change person/booth cashier wipes down the bank of machines in the assigned zone: screens, button decks, bill validators, card readers, coin trays, machine tops and the stools/chairs, using a sanitizing cloth, working around seated patrons and their drinks, players' cards and belongings, to casino presentation standards.

Cleaning the change booth / cage workstation itself at shift change: wiping the counter, the glass window and pass-through, the ticket printer/coin counter surfaces and keyboard, removing coin dust, ticket stubs and wrappers, and emptying the booth wastebasket inside a locked, camera-covered cage.

Policing the assigned area for litter between transactions: collecting abandoned cups, bottles and glassware from machine ledges and chairs, picking up napkins, spent TITO tickets and wrappers from the carpet, and emptying ashtrays and small trash receptacles, while distinguishing litter from patrons' active drinks and belongings.

Responding to a spot mess during the shift: a spilled drink on the carpet and machine console, a dumped ashtray, or sticky residue on a button deck; blotting/wiping it up promptly with towels and cleaner, placing a caution sign if needed, so play can resume within a minute or two amid patrons.

Light floor care of the assigned area, mostly on graveyard or before opening in a smaller casino: dust-mopping or sweeping the hard floor around the booth and cage, running a vacuum down the carpeted slot aisles, and removing debris before the shift changes.

Car, truck and trailer rental (Enterprise, Hertz, U-Haul): walk-around inspection of the vehicle for dents, scratches, tire and glass condition, fuel/charge and cleanliness; prep to the customer's need — move seats and mirrors, fit or remove a child seat, ski rack, hand controls or hitch ball/wiring for a trailer, verify trailer lights and coupler fit to the customer's vehicle in the lot.

Ski/snowboard rental counter fitting: measure the customer's foot and boot sole length, size boots, pull skis/board sized to the skier, set binding toe and heel to boot sole length and forward pressure, set DIN/release value from weight, height, age and ability, run the release/ISO check, and inspect bases and edges for damage before hand-off; peak-hour queue in a shop fitting area.

Ski/snowboard rental fleet turnaround and pre-season servicing in the shop's back workshop: inspect returned skis/boards for base gouges and dull or burred edges, grind edges and base and wax them to the program matched to the renter class (beginner/sport/race), so the item is ready to meet the next customer's needs.

Bicycle, e-bike, scooter, kayak/paddleboard and other recreation rental: adjust saddle height and handlebar/stem reach to the rider, check and set tire pressure, test brakes and shifting, add or move a child seat or basket, size and fit a helmet or PFD; done at a shop door or beachfront kiosk with the customer present.

Party/event, formalwear, home medical and furniture/appliance rental: inspect linens, chairs, tables, tents, glassware, tuxedos, crutches, walkers or wheelchairs for stains, damage and missing parts, and adjust them to the customer — hem/size a garment, set crutch or walker height and wheelchair footrests, swap legs or covers, assemble a table or canopy to the ordered configuration.
