tasks.label: Explain products or services and prices and demonstrate use of products.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: In-home door-to-door product demonstration: the seller is invited into a private residence and sets up and physically operates a consumer product (vacuum cleaner, cookware set, water-filtration unit, knife set, air purifier) on the customer's own carpet or kitchen, explaining features, model options and price tiers while adapting to the household's layout, clutter, pets and objections.

Doorstep canvassing for services (internet/TV, solar, home security, pest control, energy supplier, lawn care): the rep works a residential route, knocks, engages a stranger at the door, explains plan tiers, contract terms and prices, shows collateral or a tablet/app and points out installed equipment, in variable weather and with unpredictable reception.

Street/sidewalk vending from a cart, table or hand-carry (food, drinks, newspapers, flowers, phone accessories, souvenirs): calling out to passing pedestrians, naming items and prices, showing how a novelty gadget or accessory works, handing goods over and taking cash or phone payment amid traffic, crowds and weather.

Outdoor market, street fair or flea-market booth: vendor staffs a stall, explains product lines and prices to browsers, hands out food samples or runs a hands-on demo of a kitchen gadget or tool, restocks the display, and copes with wind, uneven ground and booth layouts that differ site to site.

Indoor kiosk, showroom or in-store/event demonstrator: a staffed mall kiosk, retail-floor demo table, dealership showroom or expo stand where the worker explains products and prices to walk-up shoppers and runs a repeated demonstration of the product (brewing a sample, running the appliance, showing features on the display model).

sources.title: Groundbreaking: AiMOGA Robotics' Humanoid Robot Becomes World's First to Autonomously Open Car Doors
sources.claim: AiMOGA's Mornine humanoid autonomously opens car doors inside working Chery dealerships and, per the same release, is operating in several Chery 4S dealerships assisting with customer greeting, vehicle introduction and item delivery.
sources.transferJustification: Same task family: explaining a product to a walk-up customer and physically demonstrating it (opening the vehicle) on the seller's premises, with comparable object sizes and precision.

sources.title: INTELLIGENT AIMOGA ROBOT ARRIVES IN MALAYSIA, ENHANCING CUSTOMER EXPERIENCE ACROSS MULTIPLE SCENARIOS
sources.claim: Chery states the AiMOGA robot conducts vehicle introductions, welcomes customers and guides test drives at its Malaysian dealership, switching between these tasks autonomously with multilingual interaction.
sources.transferJustification: Vehicle introduction to a prospective buyer is the same act as explaining a product and its options and price to a customer, performed inside a structured retail facility.

sources.title: Chinese Robotics Firm AiMOGA Showcases Deployment of its Car Dealership Humanoid Robot
sources.claim: About 220 Mornine units were delivered to Chery's dealer network, where the robots support showroom operations by greeting visitors, demonstrating vehicle features ....
sources.transferJustification: Demonstrating product features and answering spec/price questions in a showroom is the in-facility form of this task; scale of deployment shown, autonomy established by the developer release.

sources.title: Cheers to AI: ADAM Robot Bartender Makes Drinks at Vegas Golden Knights Game
sources.claim: Richtech's ADAM dual-arm robot staffs a customer-facing beverage station at T-Mobile Arena in Las Vegas, perceiving cups and liquid levels and adapting its actions in real time rather than replaying a fixed script.
sources.transferJustification: Transfer from beverage service: at a purpose-built station the robot operates equipment in front of walk-up customers, the same physical act as running a fixtured product demonstration at a demo booth.

sources.title: This Humanoid Robot, Powered in Part by NVIDIA, is Ready to Serve Espresso Drinks
sources.claim: ADAM operated a commercial coffee kiosk in a Las Vegas shopping mall under the Clouffee and Tea brand, preparing coffee and serving desserts to paying customers, and later worked venues such as Globe Life Field.
sources.transferJustification: Mall-kiosk vending of prepared goods to walk-up customers matches the kiosk and street-vending instances when those arise inside a structured facility.

sources.title: Richtech Robotics Humanoid Robot Starts Serving Coffee in Georgia; Nvidia AI
sources.claim: ADAM units serving coffee in Georgia use voice AI to accept commands in multiple languages and recommend drinks to customers, with human associates only on hand to help customers interact.
sources.transferJustification: Describing and recommending menu items to a customer is the verbal half of explaining products and prices, done by the same machine that then makes the product.

sources.title: Pepper the Robot Is Coming to Work in U.S. Retail Stores, and Then Your Home
sources.claim: SoftBank's Pepper robot was deployed in customer-facing product-explanation roles in Nissan showrooms, Nescafe coffee-machine stores and SoftBank Mobile stores, and helped shoppers select wine at Carrefour.
sources.transferJustification: Directly the verbal core of this task - explaining products, specifications and plans to customers - carried out by a robot standing on retail premises.

sources.title: Nestlé to use humanoid robot to sell Nescafé in Japan
sources.claim: Nestle Japan contracted Pepper robots to sell Nescafe coffee machines in home-appliance stores, scaling toward roughly 1,000 stores, i.e. a robot staffing the product-explanation and sales role for a consumer appliance.
sources.transferJustification: Selling a consumer appliance in-store requires explaining the product and its price, the verbal component of this task, in an institution-controlled facility.

sources.title: New Helix Video Shows Robot Loading and Unloading Dishwasher Pretty Damn Well
sources.claim: Figure's Helix 02 completed a four-minute end-to-end autonomous household task - walking to a dishwasher, ... it, stacking items in cabinets, then ... appliance - with no resets or human intervention, in the developer's staged home setting.
sources.transferJustification: Related task (household appliance operation): shows autonomous operation of a consumer appliance, the manipulation core of demonstrating an appliance, but only in the developer's staged home with no customer present.

Street food/beverage cart vendor: assembles or cooks the order to request (hot dog, taco, coffee, shaved ice), hands the food across the cart to the customer and takes payment on the spot, at a curbside pitch on a public street.

Door-to-door delivery of pre-ordered small merchandise to private homes (cosmetics/Avon orders, cookies, catalog goods, household products): walk up the path and steps, knock, hand the parcel to the customer at the door or leave it, and collect payment (cash, check, or card reader).
Newspaper/periodical route delivery to houses and small businesses along a residential route, with occasional in-person collection of subscription payments at the door.

Vending from a truck/van door-to-door in neighborhoods with bulkier goods (produce boxes, seafood, water, household goods): carry cases from the vehicle to the door or into the kitchen/garage, and take payment on a handheld terminal or in cash.

Selling and handing over merchandise at an institution-controlled venue: hawking programs, drinks or souvenirs in stadium/arena aisles and concourses, a convention hall, an airport concourse, a campus, or an indoor fairground/market; carry goods to patrons and take card or cash payment.

sources.title: Bridging the 'Porch Gap'

instances.label: A door-to-door representative for a home service (solar, pest control, alarm monitoring, fiber internet) works a residential block on a weekday evening: walking driveways, lawns, porch steps and gates, ringing doorbells, sizing up whoever answers, delivering a pitch, handling objections and loose dogs, and closing a signed agreement on a tablet.

A direct-sales distributor or route seller travels by car, bicycle or on foot to deliver ordered merchandise (cosmetics, household products, snack/candy orders, papers and circulars) to customers' homes and workplaces across a service area, parking, carrying the item to the door, and collecting payment or leaving the drop.

A street food vendor hauls a hot-dog, taco or coffee cart to a sidewalk or plaza pitch, sets up, cooks and assembles orders to order for walk-up customers through a lunch rush in whatever weather, takes cash and card, restocks, and packs out at the end of the shift.

A sidewalk, park or event vendor sells packaged goods - bottled water, snacks, cut fruit, flowers, souvenirs, newspapers - from a cart, folding table, cooler or tray, moving to the day's pitch and circulating among pedestrians, approaching passersby, quoting prices and taking payment.

An ice cream truck or mobile vendor truck circulates residential streets on a summer afternoon, pulling over when flagged down, serving packaged novelties and drinks through the window, taking cash, then driving on to the next block or park entrance.

A vendor circulates inside an institution-controlled venue - an airport concourse, arena concourse, hotel or office building, or campus - carrying snacks, drinks or merchandise to customers where they are, or bringing an ordered item to a waiting customer, and completing payment.

sources.transferJustification: Related task: home grocery delivery. It matches the 'travel to deliver merchandise to customers' homes' instance - residential streets taken as found, ordinary retail goods, handover to the household.

sources.claim: DoorDash's Dot robot drives autonomously on public roads, bike lanes, sidewalks and driveways at up to 20 mph to bring orders to customers in the Phoenix metro area.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: road-going last-mile delivery. Transfers to the 'travel by automobile to deliver merchandise' instances - the vehicle drives ordinary public roads and residential driveways unattended and completes the handover to the customer.

sources.system: Neolix L4 unmanned vehicle (mobile vending configuration)
sources.title: Meet the company behind China's self-driving vending machines: Inside China's Startups
sources.claim: Neolix unmanned Level 4 vehicles are used as roaming mobile vending machines in parks and scenic areas, where pedestrians flag the vehicle down, scan a code and buy beverages on the spot.
sources.transferJustification: Direct match rather than transfer: a self-driving vehicle circulating among pedestrians and selling packaged drinks to walk-up buyers is the mobile street-vending instance of this task.

sources.title: Ottonomy Unveils Ottobot; The World's First Fully Autonomous Delivery Robot Delivering in Both Indoor and Outdoor Environments
sources.claim: Ottonomy's Ottobot navigates a busy airport terminal fully autonomously to bring food and travel-retail items to passengers where they are waiting.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: in-terminal food and retail delivery. Transfers to the 'circulate among potential customers inside a venue to deliver merchandise' instance - same crowded concourse, same small merchandise, same customer handover.

sources.title: Hotel Delivery Robot Deployed in Los Angeles, California
sources.claim: Relay hotel service robots make room-service and amenity deliveries to guest doors with fully autonomous self-driving navigation, in commercial hotel deployments.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: room-service item delivery in hotels. Transfers to the in-venue vendor instance - the robot travels corridors and elevators of a human-occupied facility to bring goods to a customer's door and complete the handover.

tasks.label: Set up and display sample merchandise at parties or stands.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: In-home party display: a direct-sales consultant (cosmetics, kitchenware, jewelry) arrives at a host's private home, clears and dresses the host's dining/coffee table with a cloth, unpacks a sample kit, arranges samples attractively by product line, sets out catalogs, order forms and price cards, and adjusts the layout to the room's furniture and lighting.

Outdoor street/sidewalk or farmers-market stand: vendor unloads from a vehicle or cart, erects a pop-up canopy and folding tables, weights/stakes it against wind, drapes covers, stacks and arranges produce or crafts into piles and tiers, hangs banner and hand-written price signs, and re-adjusts through the day for weather and passers-by.

Indoor mall concourse or transit-station kiosk/cart: vendor opens a leased cart, unlocks and loads display cases and pegboards with small merchandise (phone accessories, sunglasses, candles), sets samples for handling, places signage and card reader, and faces stock during the shift.

Sample/demo table inside a host facility (in-store demo, trade show, community expo booth): vendor sets a skirted table in an assigned booth space, arranges sample merchandise, literature and a giveaway display, sets up a small backdrop or banner stand, and keeps the display replenished and tidy.

News/periodical stand: vendor opens a corner stand or transit-station stall at dawn, cuts bundles, stacks newspapers and magazines into racks and on the counter face-out by title, clips display copies against wind, and adds impulse items (candy, drinks) along the front.

sources.title: Amazon introduces Sparrow—a state-of-the-art robot that handles millions of diverse products
sources.claim: Amazon's Sparrow robotic arm autonomously identifies and handles a very wide range of individual consumer products, picking them from totes and placing them into other containers inside fulfillment centers.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: bin picking of diverse retail merchandise. Setting up a sample display is fundamentally grasping assorted consumer goods and placing them in designated positions; Sparrow shows autonomous handling of the same object class in a purpose-built cell.

sources.title: Robotic Packaging | Automate Your Packaging & Processing
sources.claim: Vision-guided delta-robot packaging cells commercially pick assorted products and place them into trays and cartons, including assembling variety/assorted packs, i.e. arranging mixed products into a presentation layout.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: tray loading / variety-pack assembly. Arranging sample merchandise into an orderly display on a presented fixture is the same pick-and-place-into-a-defined-layout operation with comparable objects and precision, when the work is brought to the machine.

sources.system: Danfoss Drives kitting cell with Roboception rc_visard 3D vision
sources.title: Case Studies: Automated Kitting Solution with 3D Robot Vision
sources.claim: A production kitting cell with 3D vision has a robot assemble an assortment of different parts ... from supplier pallets into trays, handling variable part presentation.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: robotic kitting. Building a sample display is assembling an assortment of distinct items into a defined arrangement on a tray/board; the cited cell does this autonomously in a purpose-built cell with vision handling imperfect part presentation.

sources.title: ACPaQ Robotic Mixed Case Palletizer - Picking Solutions - Swisslog Global
sources.claim: Robotic mixed-case palletizing systems autonomously build store-ready pallets, sequencing and placing mixed SKUs into a specified stacked arrangement for retail presentation.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: building store-ready display pallets. Stacking bundled goods (newspapers, boxed stock) into a stable, presentable arrangement is the same placement problem at comparable precision, performed autonomously in a fenced cell.

sources.system: NTU Singapore autonomous IKEA chair assembly system (Denso arms)
sources.title: Robotic System Autonomously Assembles an IKEA Chair
sources.claim: Two six-axis industrial arms with 3D vision and force sensing autonomously assembled an IKEA chair from loose parts on a bench, planning motions and locating parts themselves.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: assembly of a furniture frame from presented parts. Erecting a folding table or canopy frame at a stand is a comparable multi-part structural assembly; at E1 the parts would be presented fixtured as in this bench demo.

sources.title: Telexistence Deploys AI and Remote-Controlled Robots in 300 Convenience Stores, Utilizing Azure | Microsoft Customer Stories
sources.claim: Telexistence's TX SCARA is installed in convenience-store backrooms where it autonomously detects depleted beverage shelves and replenishes/faces product on the display shelves, with remote human teleoperation only as a fallback when autonomous stocking fails; deployed at roughly 300 FamilyMart stores.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: stocking/facing merchandise on retail display shelves inside a human work facility. It shows the nearest E2 capability, but it is a fixed rail installation restricted to uniform bottled drinks, so it does not extend to setting up a varied sample display.

sources.system: "From Pixels to Shelf" autonomous supermarket stocking mobile manipulator
sources.title: From Pixels to Shelf: An Integrated Robotic System for Autonomous Supermarket Stocking with a Mobile Manipulator
sources.claim: A 2026 integrated mobile-manipulator system for autonomous supermarket shelf stocking and fronting achieved 98% pick-and-place success, but only in laboratory conditions replicating a supermarket with ArUco markers, and the authors state current autonomous performance and cost remain inferior to human workers.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: in-store merchandise stocking and fronting by a mobile robot. It is the closest analogue to setting up a display inside a real retail facility, and its lab-only, marker-dependent validation plus the authors' own comparison to human workers bound the E2 judgment.

tasks.label: Order or purchase supplies.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Street food/beverage vendor's restock run: drive to a cash-and-carry wholesaler (Restaurant Depot, Costco Business) or supermarket, push a flatbed cart through public aisles selecting 40-80 mixed items (cases of buns, sodas, condiments, produce, propane, gloves, napkins), judging dates/quality and unit prices against a budget, pay at checkout, load the van, then unload at the commissary or curbside cart.

Merchandise street vendor (souvenirs, phone cases, jewelry, T-shirts) buying resale inventory at wholesale-district shops or a jobbers' market: inspecting goods, haggling over price and quantity, paying cash, then hauling loose boxes and bags on a hand truck along crowded sidewalks to a parked vehicle.

Direct-sales rep (Avon, Mary Kay, Cutco, Tupperware) placing the campaign order through the company portal or by phone, then receiving the delivered cartons at home, checking contents against the invoice, unpacking, and sorting products, samples and brochures into per-customer bags for delivery.

News/periodical vendor or hawker: pre-dawn pickup of the day's draw at the distributor's depot dock or a street drop point, counting and signing for bundles, paying or charging the account, loading them into a car or hand cart, and returning unsold copies for credit.

Quick consumable errand between selling shifts: stop at a big-box/grocery/hardware store or bank for bags, receipt paper, batteries, bagged ice, a propane exchange or a roll of coins; select a handful of items, pay at self-checkout, and carry them to the vehicle or cart.

sources.system: Symbotic automated case-handling system (SymBots, robotic depalletizing/palletizing cells)
sources.title: Flexible Fully Autonomous Warehouse Platform | Symbotic
sources.claim: Symbotic's commercially deployed warehouse system uses fleets of vision-guided autonomous robots to induct, store, retrieve and palletize mixed-SKU cases of the same grocery/consumer goods a vendor buys wholesale, assembling a complete order pallet for dispatch inside a purpose-built robotic structure.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: wholesale grocery order assembly. It is the physical core of 'purchase supplies' when the work is brought to the machine — the ordered case quantities are selected, consolidated and staged for the buyer — with the same object class (cases of food, drinks, paper goods) and no greater precision demand than a vendor's restock run.

sources.title: Associated Foods teams up with Symbotic for warehouse automation | Supply Chain Dive
sources.claim: Grocery wholesaler Associated Food Stores contracted Symbotic to build mixed-SKU pallets for supplying independent grocers, showing the case-picking system operating on real wholesale supply orders rather than in a lab.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: assembling a wholesale supply order for a retail customer. Same goods (grocery and paper supplies) and same output (a consolidated order ready to load) that a vendor obtains on a purchasing trip.

sources.system: Symbotic system in Walmart regional distribution centers
sources.title: Walmart to Expand Deployment of Symbotic Supply Chain Automation to 25 Distribution Centers - Robotics 24/7
sources.claim: Walmart has expanded Symbotic automation across its regional distribution network, indicating the case-picking/order-building technology is in sustained production use at scale, not a one-off pilot.
sources.transferJustification: Same related task as above (supply order picking and palletizing); cited to establish deployment maturity of the system used for the E1 judgments.

sources.title: Amazon robotics: Meet the robots inside fulfillment centers
sources.claim: Amazon's Sparrow robotic arm autonomously picks individual, varied consumer items out of containers and places them into specific totes for customer orders inside fenced fulfillment-center cells — the item-level analogue of unpacking a shipment and sorting products into per-customer bags.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: piece-level order aggregation. A direct-sales rep's supply handling — unpack the received carton and sort individual cosmetics/small goods into per-customer bags — involves the same object class, grasp precision, and sort-to-destination logic Sparrow performs in production.

sources.developer: Boston Dynamics (deployed by DHL Supply Chain)
sources.title: From case unloading to picking and beyond with DHL and Boston Dynamics - Automated Warehouse
sources.claim: Boston Dynamics' Stretch autonomously detects, grasps and places boxes of varying size and type without pre-programming, and is commercially deployed unloading trailers and containers for DHL, showing autonomous handling of unfixtured cases arriving as a supply shipment.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: receiving and breaking down an inbound supply shipment. Handling mixed, unfixtured cartons of consumer goods matches the receiving leg of a vendor's supply purchase; Boston Dynamics' in-aisle order-building for Stretch is still described as under development, so it supports only the dock/receiving portion.

sources.system: Digit humanoid robot with Agility Arc
sources.title: GXO Signs Industry-First Multi-Year Agreement with Agility Robotics | Agility
sources.claim: Agility Robotics' Digit humanoid is under a commercial RaaS agreement with GXO moving totes in a working fulfillment facility, the closest deployed case of a mobile robot doing material handling in a human-standard warehouse; it moves standardized totes on fixed workflows and does not shop, select or pay for goods.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: repetitive tote/case movement in a human-occupied facility. Cited to bound the E2 judgment: the deployed capability is fixed tote workflows, not selecting varied merchandise from store shelves, judging quality, paying, and hauling it to a vending site.

tasks.label: Stock carts or stands.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Street food/beverage cart vendor (hot dog, halal, taco, coffee cart): loads the cart at a commissary or from a van each morning — cases of soda, water, buns, wrapped food, condiment bottles, paper goods, bagged ice, propane — then tops it up curbside from a cooler or storage box during the day.

Newsstand/sidewalk kiosk operator: cuts bundles of newspapers and magazines, slots and faces them on racks, and refills shelf and cooler stock with candy, snacks, cigarettes and bottled drinks in a cramped kiosk.

Farmers'/flea market or sidewalk table vendor: unloads crates from a vehicle, sets up tables and canopy, arranges produce or merchandise into display piles/baskets, and replenishes and re-faces the display as it sells down, in outdoor weather.

Mobile concession/hawker cart in a stadium, arena, or airport concourse: draws cases of drinks, snacks, ice and condiments from a stockroom, wheels them to the cart, loads bins and coolers, and re-stocks between innings/flights under time pressure.

Ice cream / frozen-novelty push-cart or mobile retail vendor: at a depot freezer, loads boxed novelties and dry ice or ice into the cart's insulated wells, checks counts, and re-loads mid-route from a chase vehicle.

sources.title: Restocking robots deployed in 300 Japanese convenience stores - The Robot Report
sources.claim: Telexistence's TX SCARA is deployed in 300 FamilyMart convenience stores ..., where it works inside the store's cold compartment and replenishes beverage display shelves around the clock — a store-shelf stocking job in a human retail facility.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: restocking a refrigerated retail display with bottles/cans. Transfers partially to stocking a vendor stand with packaged drinks — comparable objects and placement precision — but the robot is a fixed installation serving one known display, not a mobile worker loading a cart.

sources.title: Telexistence develops a new robot TX SCARA and installs it at FamilyMart METI Store
sources.claim: TX SCARA runs autonomously under its 'Gordon' AI during normal operation, with a remote human operator taking over only to recover from occasional restocking failures.
sources.transferJustification: Establishes autonomy (with rare remote assist) for the retail shelf-restocking evidence above.

sources.title: ACPaQ Robotic Mixed Case Palletizer - Picking Solutions - Swisslog
sources.claim: Swisslog/KUKA's ACPaQ robotic cell autonomously builds mixed-SKU, store-friendly pallets from single-SKU inbound stock in grocery distribution centres — i.e., a fenced machine cell that assembles a mixed load of cases in a chosen sequence.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: building a mixed-case store order. Loading a vendor cart or stand at a fixtured station is the same operation — retrieving assorted cases of packaged goods and placing them in a required arrangement on a defined load carrier.

sources.title: Amazon's Vulcan robot uses force sensing to stow items - The Robot Report
sources.claim: Amazon's Vulcan robots stow diverse retail items into the small compartments of fabric storage pods in live fulfillment centres in Spokane and Hamburg, handling roughly three quarters of the item catalogue at human-comparable speed.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: stowing heterogeneous consumer goods into filled compartments. Stocking a cart's bins or a stand's shelves with assorted packaged merchandise involves the same objects, contact-rich insertion, and comparable precision, when the receptacle is presented in a known position.

sources.title: Chef Robotics completes 100M meal servings milestone - The Robot Report
sources.claim: Chef Robotics' AI-driven arms fill trays with assorted food ingredients on production lines in more than a dozen food facilities in North America and Europe, passing 100 million servings, and the same piece-picking models place whole fruits into clamshells and snack boxes.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: filling trays/containers with food items and produce on a line. Stocking a food cart's pans, bins and coolers with the same class of food goods is equivalent handling when items are presented at a fixed station.

sources.title: Yummy Fruit's produce packing robot reaches 20M apples milestone
sources.claim: The Aporo packing robot uses vision and a multi-head picker to place apples into display trays in commercial packhouses, having placed over 20 million apples for one grower.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: gentle placement of loose fruit into an ordered display tray. A market stand's produce display is the same object class and placement quality, when fruit and trays are presented by a purpose-built line.

sources.title: Zippy Ice Speeds Up Bagging with Robotic Palletizing - FANUC America
sources.claim: A FANUC robotic palletizing cell took over the manual job of stacking bags of ice at Zippy Ice, showing robotic handling of heavy, floppy bagged ice in a cold environment.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: handling bagged ice. Loading ice into a vending cart's well is the same object and grip problem; this shows the awkward, heavy, deformable items in cart stocking are handled in fixtured cells.

sources.title: Fully Automated Palletizing in Cold Storage at -25 °C | KUKA Global
sources.claim: KUKA Arctic palletizing robots operate continuously inside a -25 °C deep-freeze store, moving frozen goods in a fenced automated cell.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: case handling in a freezer. Loading boxed frozen novelties into an ice-cream cart at a depot involves the same cases and temperatures, when presented at a fixtured station.

sources.title: Agility Robotics' Digit humanoid passes 100,000-tote milestone in live GXO implementation
sources.claim: Agility Robotics' Digit humanoid has moved more than 100,000 ... commercial operation at GXO's Flowery Branch facility, picking totes on and off mobile robots, loading conveyors and stacking containers — mobile material handling inside a structured logistics facility, but limited to standardized totes at engineered stations.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: mobile tote handling in a human-scale facility. Shows the current ceiling for mobile manipulation in E2 settings — uniform totes on fixed routes — which does not extend to fetching assorted merchandise and loading an unfixtured vending cart.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Reception/switchboard station in a clinic, apartment office, service business or small firm: taking a walk-in payment in cash or check, verifying the bill/account, counting the money, making change from a drawer, writing or printing a receipt and logging the payment.

Managing an office petty cash fund: disbursing small amounts of cash against vouchers/receipts to staff, replenishing the box, periodically counting bills and coins and reconciling the count to the log/receipts in a locked back-office setting.

End-of-shift/daily preparation of collected receipts for deposit: tallying loose bills, coins and checks, endorsing checks, completing a deposit slip, sealing the deposit bag, balancing to the day's payment log in the office.

Physically taking the prepared deposit to the bank: carrying the locked bag on foot or by car to a branch teller, night drop or deposit-taking ATM, handing over or inserting the deposit and returning with a receipt.

Processing mailed-in payments at an answering-service or small business office: opening envelopes, extracting and endorsing checks, matching them to accounts/remittance stubs, logging amounts and batching them for deposit.

Mailroom or back office of an office building, school, hospital, or hotel: the operator opens the day's tray of mixed incoming mail (letters, window envelopes, magazines, catalogs, padded mailers, small parcels), reads names and departments, and sorts each piece into labeled pigeonholes, department bins, or guest/resident slots, culling misdirected and bulk mail.

Distribution round: the operator loads a cart or tote with sorted mail and packages and walks a route through corridors and elevators to department mail stops, reception trays, nurse stations, or suites, dropping off items and picking up outgoing mail at each stop.

Preparing outgoing mail and shipments in a mailroom or at the front desk: folding and stuffing letters and statements into envelopes, sealing, weighing, running items through a postage meter or printing shipping labels, boxing a few items for courier shipment, and staging everything in the outgoing bin for carrier pickup.

Hospitality/healthcare variant: a package, flowers, or an amenity arrives for a hotel guest or patient; the operator logs it and carries or sends it to the guest room or patient unit, confirming receipt with the recipient.

instances.label: Office paper jam: an invoice/statement run stops on the department's laser printer or multifunction copier; the clerk opens trays, the duplexer and rear/fuser doors, locates and pulls out crumpled or partially torn sheets, checks for fragments, closes covers, clears the error and re-runs the missing pages.

Higher-volume billing/mail equipment misfeed: a folder-inserter, envelope stuffer, statement printer, remittance/check scanner or postage meter jams in a mailroom or statement-production area; the clerk opens access covers, turns knobs/levers, pulls damaged documents and envelopes out of the transport, verifies piece integrity and restarts the job with the affected pieces re-run.

Media reload: printer, inserter or label/postage device runs out of stock; the clerk fetches a ream/box, unwraps and fans it, opens the tray or feeder, loads and aligns the stack, closes the tray and resumes the job.

Other small fixes: replacing a toner/ink cartridge or printer ribbon, reseating a loose USB/network/power cable, cleaning a scanner feed roller or glass, or power-cycling a frozen scanner, terminal or receipt printer.

Major fault: repeated jams, a hardware error code, a broken feed roller or a dead device; the clerk inspects the machine, determines it is beyond a minor fix, tags it out of service and notifies the vendor/IT/facilities repair personnel with a description of the symptoms and machine ID.

Cash boxes, coin, petty cash and vouchers: event/fundraiser cash boxes, donation or collection envelopes, vending and coin route proceeds, employee expense vouchers and payment coupons are counted (loose coin and bills), reconciled to logs, recorded, and deposited.

instances.label: Chain retail store, grocery, or quick-service restaurant back office at close of business: the bookkeeping clerk/office manager takes in each cashier's drawer or drop bag, counts notes and coin, compares totals to POS shift reports, resolves over/short, prepares the deposit slip, and seals the tamper-evident bag for the armored carrier's next pickup. Institution-controlled premises, standard equipment, same layout daily.

Central cash office of a multi-outlet institution (hotel front desk plus F&B outlets, hospital cashier windows, university bursar, casino cage, stadium concessions): clerk receives drops from several cashiering points, verifies each against PMS/POS/billing reports, balances, issues floats, and assembles the consolidated deposit for vault or armored pickup. Controlled premises, fixed layout, standardized paperwork.

Professional or service-business office (medical practice, law firm, contractor, nonprofit): the day's incoming mail brings checks, some with remittance stubs, some folded inside letters, plus a few counter payments in cash and check; the clerk opens and triages the mail, endorses checks, posts payments against open invoices, runs the batch through a desktop scanner for remote deposit capture, verifies the batch total, and files copies. Ordinary office, institution-controlled.

Independent small business (single-location shop, restaurant, clinic, auto shop): clerk counts the day's register cash and checks, prepares the deposit slip and bag, then walks or drives the deposit to the bank branch or night depository and returns with the validated receipt. Work spans the office, a parking lot, public streets, and a bank lobby or drop chute.

Informal or mobile operation (food truck, farmers-market stands, festival or fundraiser, mobile service crews, small nonprofit): loose bills, coin, and checks with handwritten tally sheets are counted on whatever surface is available at varying sites, matched against ad hoc receipts, then assembled into a deposit and taken to a bank. No fixed layout or standard equipment.

tasks.label: Maintain cage security.

instances.label: Cage door access control on a casino floor: verifying badge/authorization of arriving dealers, floor supervisors, slot attendants, armored-car couriers or vendors before releasing the locked/interlocked cage door, admitting one person at a time, logging the entry, and confirming the door relocks behind them — done repeatedly through a shift under surveillance cameras.

Window bank security during the shift: keeping the imprest bank of currency, chips, tickets and markers under control at a cage window — nothing left within a patron's reach, drawer locked whenever the window is left, payouts and large bills counted in camera view, counterfeit notes detected and retained.

Shift-change and vault security: dual-control transfer and verification of the bank to and from the main vault, dropping excess cash, locking safes and drawers, and drawing/returning cage and vault keys under logged dual control at shift open and close.

Vigilance and incident response at the window: watching patrons for distraction scams, chip passing, stolen tickets or cards, laundering red flags, agitated or intoxicated persons and robbery indicators; refusing suspect transactions, discreetly signaling surveillance/security, triggering the panic alarm and following lockdown procedure.

Securing funds in motion: preparing and moving chip fills/credits, cash for kiosks and ATMs, and pouch transfers across the casino floor and back-of-house corridors with a security escort, keeping the funds under continuous control and verified at both ends.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Credit/debit card cash advance at the cage window: patron presents card and photo ID, cashier keys/swipes the card through the cash-access terminal, obtains issuer authorization, captures the patron's signature, then counts and passes several hundred to a few thousand dollars in currency through the window.

Routine check cashing for an enrolled/established patron within an existing limit: personal check or electronic check drawn on the patron's bank, verified through the casino's check-warranty service (Central Credit/VIP Preferred), patron endorses, cashier verifies ID against the account and counts out the cash.

First-time or walk-up patron wanting to cash a personal check: cashier captures driver's license/ID, runs the patron through the check-verification and enrollment service, a check-cashing limit is established, and, if approved, cash is paid out at the window.

Other standard paper instruments presented at the cage: payroll checks, government checks, cashier's checks and casino-issued checks (jackpot or front-money withdrawal checks) — instrument inspected and endorsed, amount verified, currency counted out to the patron.

Exception and judgment transactions: declined or over-limit authorizations needing a supervisor override or a call to the issuing bank, ID mismatch or suspected altered/fraudulent check, third-party, traveler's or counter-check (marker) instruments, patron disputes over fees, and large cash-outs triggering Title 31 identification, MTL entry and CTR/SAR review.

tasks.label: Convert gaming checks, coupons, tokens, or coins to currency for gaming patrons.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Table-game chip ('check') redemption at the cage window: a patron pushes across a rack or handful of mixed-denomination chips; the cashier verifies the chips are the house's genuine chips (not foreign, counterfeit, damaged or altered), counts them, records the transaction in the cage system, and counts out currency through the window. Typical value tens to a few thousand dollars.

Slot TITO voucher / gaming-check redemption at the cage: patron presents one or several barcoded slot tickets (often crumpled, sometimes several at once, sometimes rejected earlier by a kiosk for a jam or empty cassette); cashier scans and validates each in the ticketing system and pays currency.

Large-value conversion requiring identity and Title 31 handling: chips or tickets totalling above the property's threshold (commonly >$3,000 for MTL logging, >$10,000 aggregated triggering a CTR); cashier requests photo ID and SSN, records patron data, may need supervisor approval and dual verification, watches for structuring or suspicious behavior, then counts out a large sum of currency.

Promotional instruments converted at the cage: match-play or 'cash back' coupons, mailer coupons, drawing/prize slips, non-negotiable promo chips and comp/point slips; cashier checks the terms, expiry, one-per-patron eligibility and often the player's card/ID, decides what portion is payable in cash, and pays out.

Coins, tokens and odd items: buckets of coins from legacy coin-op machines, old slot tokens, soiled or damaged chips, chips issued at a sister property, or foreign-currency items; cashier runs coin through a counter or counts by hand, applies house policy on what is honored, and converts to currency.

tasks.label: Count funds and reconcile daily summaries of transactions to balance books.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Cage window cashier closes shift: counts the impress bank/drawer — strapped and loose currency by denomination, coin, racked gaming chips, TITO tickets, coupons and checks — enters totals, reconciles to the system-generated cashier accountability, documents any over/short, with a second employee verifying, inside the casino cage.

Main bank/vault cashier count at shift change: bulk strapped currency and coin, chip inventory in racks, plus fill/credit slips, markers and kiosk/ATM support funds; totals reconciled to the cage accountability report and daily transaction summaries under two-person control in the vault/cage.

Soft count: slot bill-validator cash boxes and table drop boxes wheeled to the count room, emptied, banknotes and TITO tickets counted on counting/sorting machines, totals recorded and reconciled to meter/system reads, then transferred and verified to the cage.

Kiosk, ATM and ticket-redemption machine cassette work: pulling and counting cassette contents (notes, tickets, coin), counting replenishment funds out of the vault, and reconciling counted amounts to device transaction/dispense reports in the cage back office.

Chip bank / table-fill bank inventory count: counting the cage chip inventory by denomination in racks and reconciling it to fills, credits, table inventory forms and the chip accountability record at end of gaming day.

Occurs in the cage and chip bank.

Vault / main bank currency rotation and transfers: moving strapped bundles and coin between vault and cage under dual control, running currency through counters, strapping and labeling, pulling worn or mutilated notes out of the working inventory, and preparing bank deposits or armored-car shipments. Occurs in the casino vault/cash room.

Floor device cash rotation: removing accumulated cash and vouchers from ticket-redemption kiosks and ATMs and replenishing their cassettes/dispensers with counted, verified currency, escorted by security, with reconciliation paperwork. Occurs on the casino floor among patrons and in the cage.

instances.label: Standard end-of-shift cage bank count and balance in a commercial casino cage: the cashier pulls the impressed bank drawer, runs currency by denomination through a desktop counter, counts chip inventory and a few checks/vouchers, reconciles the total to the beginning bank plus recorded transactions in the cage system, and signs the checkout sheet with a supervisor.

Main bank / vault cashier prepares the property's daily bank deposit: aggregates excess currency from cage banks, kiosks and the count room, runs it through a high-speed counter/sorter, straps and bundles by denomination, prepares the deposit slip, seals the tamper-evident bag, logs the bag serial number and stages it for the armored carrier.

Deposit preparation for negotiable paper: a batch of cashed patron checks, money orders and travelers' items is endorsed, run through a scanner or listed on an adding machine, totaled and balanced against the check-cashing log, and a check deposit (physical or remote deposit capture) is created.

Coin/token deposit preparation at a racino, bingo hall or older slot floor: mixed loose coin and tokens are run through a coin counter/sorter, bagged and tagged by denomination to Fed-standard bag values, totals reconciled to the coin log and added to the day's deposit.

Small venue single-cashier close-out (card room, bingo hall, OTB parlor, small tribal casino): one worker counts the till of currency and checks largely by hand, completes a handwritten deposit slip, seals the deposit bag and drops it in the vault or drop safe for later bank runner pickup.

Cage bank balance where the assigned fund contains heterogeneous non-cash items: outstanding markers/credit instruments, promotional coupons and match-play, foreign currency, hand-pay and jackpot slips, fill/credit slips and torn or suspect notes, all requiring itemized reconciliation and a documented, witnessed variance investigation before the deposit is released.

instances.label: Manufacturing/warehouse/food plant on a punch-clock system: at the start of the pay period the clerk loads 50-300 pre-printed individual timecards into the slotted racks beside each time clock on the plant floor; at cutoff the clerk pulls every completed card from the 'out' racks, checks for missing, torn or mis-filed cards, and batches them by department.

Office/administrative employer using paper timesheets: the clerk prints per-employee sheets and distributes them to department mailboxes, desks, or interoffice envelopes, then collects signed sheets from supervisors' in-boxes or a drop box, walking the floor to chase stragglers before the cutoff.

Large institution with departments (hospital, hotel, school district, university): the clerk carries bundles of timecards/timesheets to unit clerks or department offices at the start of the period and picks up the completed bundles at the cutoff, transporting them back to the payroll office through corridors and elevators.

Multi-site/field employer (construction, landscaping, trucking, home care): the clerk prepares and mails or couriers blank card packets to job sites and foremen, and processes returned batches (opening envelopes, extracting cards, sorting by crew); sometimes drives to a site trailer or shop to hand out and pick up cards.

Payroll/HR service window: employees come to the counter to pick up their timecard at the start of the period and hand the completed card back at the end; the clerk verifies identity, issues the correct card, receives returns, stamps/date-marks and files them.

instances.label: Manufacturing/industrial plant receiving dock: pallets and cartons of components, raw materials and MRO items arrive; clerk matches packing slip to PO, counts pieces/cartons, verifies part numbers, lot codes and certificates, checks for shipping damage, spot-checks dimensions or other spec attributes against drawings, then posts the goods receipt in the ERP and flags shortages/rejects to the supplier.

Distribution center / 3PL dock, floor-loaded trailer of uniform labeled cartons: cases are unloaded and each case label is scanned and reconciled against the ASN/PO; shortages, overages and mislabeled cases are flagged and the receipt is recorded.

Distribution center / warehouse dock, palletized or mixed freight: clerk counts pallets and cases (Ti-Hi), reads pallet and case labels, checks for crushed/wet cartons, temperature or seal integrity, reconciles to the PO and notes exceptions on the bill of lading.

Hospital, school district, or government storeroom receiving area: mixed cartons of supplies arrive from several vendors; clerk opens/verifies item numbers and quantities, checks lot numbers, expiration dates and cold-chain items, inspects for damage, receipts into the ERP and routes goods to departments.

Office or small-facility receiving (mailroom, back office, small shop): parcels dropped by carriers; clerk opens boxes, compares contents (model number, size, color, configuration) with the purchase order, confirms nothing is missing or damaged, signs the packing slip and records receipt.

Off-site delivery point taken as found — construction jobsite, remote field office, yard or curbside drop: heterogeneous materials (lumber, pipe, fittings, equipment, drums) are set down wherever the driver can reach; clerk counts bundles, checks grade stamps/markings and part tags against specs, inspects for damage, and signs or rejects the delivery outdoors.

roles.title: Tellers
roles.description: Receive and pay out money. Keep records of money and negotiable instruments involved in a financial institution's various transactions.

tasks.label: Balance currency, coin, and checks in cash drawers at ends of shifts and calculate daily transactions, using computers, calculators, or adding machines.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Retail bank branch teller at end of shift: pulls the cash drawer to the counter/back counter, counts strapped and loose currency by denomination, rolled and loose coin, and the day's checks and other deposited items; enters totals into the teller system, compares to the system's day totals, prints the settlement, and turns the drawer into the vault. Indoor branch, standard fixtures, institution controls access.

High-volume urban or commercial-services branch teller: closing out a drawer holding several thousand dollars of mixed currency from business deposits, bagged/rolled coin, and a thick batch of checks and money orders; runs currency through a desktop discriminator and coin through a sorter, balances against a long transaction journal under time pressure at close.

Head teller / vault teller performing end-of-day branch settlement: balancing the main vault cash and coin, ATM/ITM cassette counts, incoming and outgoing armored-car shipments, and aggregating each teller's proved drawer into branch daily totals and the general-ledger cash position.

Small community bank, credit union, in-store (supermarket) or drive-up teller with low daily volume: manually counting a modest drawer of currency, rolled coin and a handful of checks, footing the day's tickets on a calculator or adding machine, and proving to the teller terminal totals in a compact station.

Drawer is out of balance: teller recounts currency and coin, re-adds check totals, reviews the transaction journal, deposit tickets and receipt images or branch camera footage to locate the error (miscounted withdrawal, mis-keyed deposit, item in the wrong drawer), then makes the correcting entry and files an over/short report with the supervisor.

Drawer containing non-standard negotiables along with cash: money orders, official/cashier's checks, savings bonds, traveler's checks, foreign currency, night-drop and merchant bags left for the shift; teller must count, classify and reconcile these items into the shift's totals.

tasks.label: Receive checks and cash for deposit, verify amounts, and check accuracy of deposit slips.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Routine retail deposit at the teller window in a bank/credit-union branch lobby: a walk-in customer presents a handful of checks and/or a modest stack of currency with a deposit slip; the teller counts the cash (often on a currency counter or teller cash recycler), inspects and endorses the checks, verifies the slip total matches, posts the credit and hands back a receipt.

Drive-up lane deposit: cash, checks and a deposit slip arrive through a pneumatic tube carrier or drawer from a customer in a vehicle; the teller counts and verifies the items, reconciles to the slip, posts the deposit and returns the receipt through the tube, communicating by intercom.

Small-business/merchant counter deposit of currency and checks (no loose coin): strapped and loose bills plus a batch of business checks with an itemized deposit slip; the teller runs the cash through a counter/recycler, batches and scans the checks, reconciles totals to the slip and issues a receipt or difference notice.

Coin-heavy merchant deposit at the counter: rolled and loose coin (plus some currency) brought in bags by a retailer, laundromat or vending operator; the teller runs coin through a coin sorter/counter, weighs or counts rolls, and reconciles the total to the deposit slip.

Back-office processing of night-depository bags, ATM deposit envelopes/bins and mail deposits under dual control the next morning: open sealed tamper-evident bags, sort mixed contents (banded bills, folded currency, checks, coin, slips), count each deposit, verify against the enclosed deposit slip and post, documenting any discrepancy.

Non-conforming/exception deposit at the counter: slip total disagrees with contents, unsigned/stale-dated/third-party/foreign or mutilated items, suspect or damaged currency, a deposit at or above $10,000 requiring ID and CTR data, split deposits with cash back, or a customer who disputes the count — requires judgment, conversation with the customer and manual resolution.

tasks.label: Monitor bank vaults to ensure cash balances are correct.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Start-of-day / end-of-day branch vault balance verification: the vault teller (often under dual control) counts the currency straps, loose notes and coin bags held in the branch vault, totals them, and reconciles the physical total to the vault control record in the core system before opening or closing.

Intraday vault buys and sells: the vault teller issues straps and coin to teller drawers and takes in excess cash from drawers throughout the day, counting each transfer, keeping the running vault position correct and posting the movements so the vault balance stays accurate.

Armored-carrier shipment verification: receiving sealed bags/containers of currency straps and coin from Brink's/Loomis, verifying seals and contents against the manifest, and building/verifying outgoing shipments of excess cash, then adjusting the recorded vault balance.

Periodic dual-control or surprise vault cash audits: recounting vault currency straps and coin bags (plus ATM replenishment residuals) against the vault records on a scheduled or unannounced basis and signing off the count.

Investigating and resolving an out-of-balance vault condition: recounting, tracing the day's teller buys/sells and journals, reviewing camera or transaction records to locate the difference, and documenting the correcting entry.

tasks.label: Cash checks and pay out money after verifying that signatures are correct, that written and numerical amounts agree, and that accounts have sufficient funds.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Routine in-branch teller window: an account holder hands over a personal or payroll check (typically under $1,000), the teller inspects the endorsement/signature, confirms written and numeric amounts agree, checks the account balance and holds in the core system, counts bills out of the drawer or cash recycler, and hands over cash plus a receipt.

Drive-through lane: the check and photo ID arrive by pneumatic tube or drawer; the teller verifies signature, amounts and available funds on the terminal, counts the cash, and sends money, ID and receipt back out through the tube, often with a two-way audio/video exchange.

Large or unusual payout: a customer cashes a check for several thousand dollars; the teller verifies ID, confirms funds/hold status, may need supervisor approval and vault cash, counts and straps bills in requested denominations, and captures CTR/large-cash-transaction information.

Non-customer cashes an on-us check drawn on the bank: the teller inspects government ID, compares the drawer's signature to the signature card/image, screens for fraud or altered amounts, may take a thumbprint, collects a fee, and pays out cash.

Interactive-teller / video-teller station: the customer inserts the check at a machine in a branch vestibule or drive-up lane; the check image, amount and account status are presented to the teller, who verifies and authorizes the machine to dispense the cash and receipt.

tasks.label: Count currency, coins, and checks received, by hand or using currency-counting machine, to prepare them for deposit or shipment to branch banks or the Federal Reserve Bank.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Teller window, retail customer cash deposit: teller receives a stack of mixed-denomination bills (some worn, folded, out of face), counts it by hand or on the counter's currency counter, verifies the total against the deposit slip, and posts/stages it for deposit. Branch lobby, standard teller counter, institution-controlled premises.

Teller window/back counter, checks received: teller counts and verifies a batch of checks (1 to a few dozen) accompanying a deposit or payment, confirms amounts and endorsements, and batches/scans them for deposit or transmittal.

Start/end-of-day drawer settlement: teller counts all currency and coin in the cash drawer (loose notes, straps, rolled coin), reconciles the count to the system total, straps and turns excess cash in to the vault or head teller.

Commercial/merchant deposit at the branch back counter: bags of loose coin plus a large volume of mixed currency and checks; teller runs coin through a sorter/counter and currency through a counter, bags or rolls coin, verifies against the merchant's deposit ticket.

Preparing a cash shipment: vault teller verifies and counts currency, straps notes into standard 100-note bundles, bags and seals coin and currency, tallies and documents the shipment to the vault, another branch, or the Federal Reserve.

instances.label: Routine over-the-counter issuance in a retail bank/credit-union branch: an accountholder asks for a cashier's/official check of a few hundred to a few thousand dollars. Teller checks ID and available balance, keys payee, amount and remitter into the teller platform, debits the account plus fee, prints the item on official check stock at the teller-line MICR printer, proofreads payee/amount/serial number, logs it and hands the check and receipt to the customer.

Verifying a cashier's check presented at the window by a customer for deposit or cashing: teller physically inspects the item (issuing bank, MICR line, payee, amount, date, watermark/UV and other security features), matches endorsement and ID, decides hold or immediate availability, and captures the item for clearing; sometimes calls the issuing bank on suspicious items.

Large-value or complex issuance in the branch: real-estate closing or auto purchase check for tens or hundreds of thousands, several checks at once, or a walk-in non-customer paying cash. Requires enhanced ID/source-of-funds review, supervisor or dual-control approval and signature, CTR/AML paperwork, careful proofreading of payee spelling, and secure handoff.

Drive-up window or pneumatic-tube issuance: customer in a vehicle requests a cashier's check, sends ID and request through the tube or window; teller prepares and prints the check inside, verifies details, and returns the check, receipt and ID through the tube/drawer, often in weather and with limited visual contact.

Corrections and control work on official checks: voiding and re-issuing a misprinted or wrongly-payable check (stamping/mutilating and retaining the spoiled item, recording its serial number), plus end-of-day accounting for official check stock - counting remaining blank stock in the locked drawer, verifying serial sequence, and balancing the official check register under dual custody.

tasks.label: Identify transaction mistakes when debits and credits do not balance.

instances.label: End-of-shift drawer settlement in a retail bank branch shows a small over/short (e.g., $20). The teller works back through the day's transaction journal, receipts, and cash-in/cash-out tickets to determine which transaction was mis-keyed or given incorrect change, and reports the finding to the supervisor.

A commercial or consumer deposit does not foot: the customer's deposit slip total does not agree with the checks and cash presented. The teller identifies whether the error is an addition error on the slip, a missing or duplicated item, or an amount read incorrectly, and determines the correcting entry before posting.

Back-office proof/item-processing work: a captured batch rejects as out of balance. The operator compares captured item amounts against the control ticket and the general ledger to locate the encoding, transposition, or missing-item error and corrects the entry.

Branch settlement discrepancy involving vault, ATM, night depository, or a shared cash recycler: the teller compares general ledger entries, machine totals, and shipment/strap records to identify the offsetting posting error or miscount and where it originated.

A customer or another branch reports a discrepancy days after the fact (deposit credited to the wrong account, wrong amount posted). The teller researches archived transaction records, check images, and receipts to identify the mistake and initiate an adjustment.

Central proof / item-processing department: bulk sorting of checks and deposit tickets received in cash letters from many branches, run on a reader/sorter into pockets by routing number and item type, with reject repair, bundling, labelling and staging for clearing and archive. tasks.label: Issue checks to bond owners in settlement of transactions.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Routine over-the-counter issuance: a bond owner at the teller window (after redeeming paper savings bonds or settling a small securities/bond transaction) asks for the proceeds as an official/cashier's check. The teller keys the transaction into the core system, prints the check on branch MICR check stock, validates/logs it in the official-check register, and hands it over with a receipt. Typical amounts a few hundred to a few thousand dollars.

Larger-dollar counter issuance inside a bank branch: redemption/settlement proceeds of roughly $10k+ paid by official check, requiring identity verification of the presenter and a second approval or countersignature under the bank's dual-control policy before the printed check is released to the owner. Physically identical output; the extra steps are approval workflow and ID checking.

Non-routine counter case: the payee is an estate executor, surviving co-owner, guardian or attorney-in-fact, or the bond registration is irregular/damaged. The teller must examine and copy supporting legal paper (death certificate, letters testamentary, POA), obtain or verify a medallion signature guarantee stamp, then issue and hand over the check.

Back-office/operations batch settlement run: checks for many bond holders (matured issues, coupon/interest payments) are printed in a secure production run, matched with the correct advice/statement page, folded, inserted into window envelopes, sealed, metered and trayed for outgoing mail from the institution's operations or print-mail center.

Single check for an owner who is not present (mail-in redemption request or check ordered by phone): the teller prints the check, prepares a cover letter and envelope, sometimes certified/registered mail, records it in the official-check log, and routes it to the branch's outgoing mail.

instances.label: Incoming mail at a business office/mailroom contains customer checks and money orders sent in response to billing or collection letters: clerk opens envelopes, separates check from remittance advice/letter, logs each payment to the correct account, restrictively endorses, batches them, and locks the batch in a cash box or file safe pending deposit.

Payments arrive electronically (ACH, card, customer web portal, bank lockbox file): clerk verifies each amount posted to the correct account in the AR system, researches and corrects misapplied or short payments, and confirms funds are in the company account. No physical money or paper is handled.

A customer comes to the office counter or window to settle a delinquent account and pays in cash, money order, or check: clerk counts and inspects the money, issues a receipt, records the payment to the account in the billing system, and secures the money in a locked cash drawer.

End of day in the back office: clerk counts the cash and checks accumulated during the day, reconciles the total against the day's payment log/system totals, resolves any over/short, completes a deposit slip, seals the funds in a tamper-evident bag, and locks it in the office safe.

Moving the prepared deposit out of the clerk's custody: carrying the sealed bag across a parking lot or public street to the bank branch or night depository, or to an internal cash office/vault, or handing it to an armored courier and signing the chain-of-custody log.

instances.label: Ad hoc single pieces in a general office: clerk prints a 1-5 page reply plus a few pages of supporting records from a case/billing system, folds them, stuffs a #10 window or 9x12 envelope, completes the certified mail label (PS Form 3800 or an online barcoded coversheet), weighs and meters postage, logs the tracking number, and puts the piece in outgoing mail. Recurring batch of 20-300 uniform certified notices (delinquent account letters, claim denials, cancellation notices) of 2-10 pages each, produced in an office mailroom: print, collate by addressee, fold, insert, seal, apply certified barcodes, meter postage, and log tracking numbers to a firm mailing book (PS Form 3877).

Records that exist only as paper originals in file cabinets: retrieve the file, remove staples and clips, photocopy or scan-and-print the set, re-collate and re-fasten, return originals to the file, then assemble the copy set with a cover letter into a certified mail envelope.

High-volume certified mailing (500-20,000 pieces) of statutorily required notices with attached records, produced in-house on production mail equipment or handed to a print-and-mail vendor, using barcoded certified labels, electronic return receipt, and an electronic manifest of tracking numbers.

The clerk searches the electronic records management system, agenda/ordinance database, and permit software, and answers by email or at the counter with a copy or citation.

A council member, city manager, department head, or city attorney asks for background on past municipal action: prior council votes, resolutions, contracts, easements, or an ordinance's amendment history. A title company, attorney, surveyor, or realtor requests historical property records: deeds, plats, subdivision files, assessment rolls, street vacations, code-enforcement history. The clerk works from grantor/grantee or parcel indexes, pulls microfilm or bound volumes from the vault, verifies the correct instrument, and provides certified or plain copies.

A genealogist, historian, journalist, or student requests older archival material: vital-record registers, cemetery records, census or tax ledgers, historic photographs, or century-old council minutes held in offsite or basement storage. The clerk interprets an ambiguous request, searches finding aids and paper indexes, retrieves fragile originals, and reports findings or supplies scans.

A broad public-records/FOIA-style request requiring research across several record series and formats (email archives, permit files, litigation and personnel files) with statutory deadlines. The clerk scopes the request with the requester, searches each system, assembles responsive records, flags exempt material for legal review, and issues the response with a log.

instances.label: At a driver-licensing/DMV or municipal service counter, an applicant hands over a foreign passport (often with a visa page) as proof of identity/lawful status for a license, ID card, marriage license or permit. The clerk inspects the data page and security features (laminate, UV printing, MRZ, hologram), compares the photo to the bearer, and accepts or refers the document.

An applicant presents a USCIS-issued immigration card at the counter — Permanent Resident Card (I-551), Employment Authorization Document (I-766), or Border Crossing Card. The clerk checks card version, laminate/holographic features, tactile printing and the machine-readable back, and decides whether the card is genuine and unaltered.

An applicant presents a foreign driver's license, foreign national ID card, or a consular identification card (e.g., matrícula consular). The clerk must recognize an unfamiliar credential from a reference guide/template library, judge whether its security features are consistent with the genuine issue, and accept or reject it.

Paper immigration and civil documents presented in person: I-94 printouts, I-797 approval notices, naturalization/citizenship certificates, foreign birth or marriage certificates on security paper with raised or inked registrar seals, plus notarized translations. The clerk checks seals, paper, wording, certification stamps and often cross-checks a database (SAVE/EVVE) or calls the issuing authority.

Copies or scans arriving by mail, e-mail or an online portal (photocopied passports, green cards, certificates attached to a license or filing application). Envelopes are opened and documents imaged; the clerk reviews the image for signs of alteration, mismatched fonts, or bad copies and cross-checks records, with no original available for tactile/UV inspection.

An escalated suspect case: the document looks altered, laminate is lifted, photo substituted, or the credential is unknown. The clerk works it under a UV lamp, loupe and retroreflective viewer, consults ID checking guides, contacts the issuing consulate or state investigators, documents the finding and refers it to law enforcement.

tasks.label: Perform general office activities, such as typing, answering telephones, operating office machines, processing mail, or securing confidential materials.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Keyboarding and data entry at a desk workstation in an office (law firm, clinic, agency): typing correspondence, file labels, index/metadata entries into a records or EMR system from paper source documents.
Answering the file-room or department telephone: picking up calls, taking messages, routing callers, logging record requests, all at a desk phone/headset in an office.

Operating office machines: photocopying and scanning multi-page files (removing staples/clips, loading the feeder, clearing jams, reassembling and refastening), printing labels, sending faxes, and running confidential paper through a cross-cut shredder in an office copy room.

Processing mail: collecting incoming mail and small parcels, sorting by recipient/department into pigeonholes, slitting envelopes, date-stamping and matching contents to files, and preparing outgoing envelopes/packages with postage in an office mailroom.

Making the internal delivery run: transporting a batch of mail, file folders, and records boxes on a cart between the mailroom/file room and departments or floors of the same building, where receiving staff take the items.

Securing confidential materials: refiling sensitive records into locked cabinets or a secure records room, logging check-out/return chain of custody, boxing files for secure archive storage, and placing documents in locked destruction bins.

tasks.label: Eliminate outdated or unnecessary materials, destroying them or transferring them to inactive storage, according to file maintenance guidelines or legal requirements.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Departmental office records room: clerk works cabinets/open shelves, reads folder labels and contents against the retention schedule, pulls folders whose retention has expired, removes clips/fasteners and bindings, and feeds them to a shredder or locked shred console; must not pull anything under legal hold, and works around desks and staff traffic.

Healthcare, legal, or government active file room: clerk pulls closed patient charts / case files / claim jackets from open-shelf color-coded filing, verifies closure and eligibility in the records system, packs them into cartons, labels and indexes each carton, and stages them on a dock for pickup to inactive or off-site storage.

Commercial records center / agency warehouse: destruction-eligible cartons flagged by the inventory system, pulled from multi-level racking with order pickers, barcode-verified against the destruction list and legal-hold flags, palletized, and run through an industrial shredding/baling line with certificates of destruction issued.

Modern hybrid office: purge is mostly electronic (applying retention rules in an EDMS/shared drive), plus a modest residue of paper duplicates and scanned-and-verified originals that must be physically pulled from a few cabinets and shredded or bagged for the shred vendor.

Ad hoc cleanout at a satellite office, storage closet, basement, trailer, or vacated staff office: unindexed legacy material of mixed type (banker's boxes, three-ring binders, bound ledgers, microfiche, X-ray film, diskettes, some non-records), layout and condition differ site to site, clerk judges item by item and hauls loads out to shred bins/recycling.

sources.system: Ripcord robotic digitization workcells (Hayward, CA factory)
sources.title: Ripcord uses robotics to digitize records, processes and avoid paper waste
sources.claim: Ripcord runs a purpose-built robotic digitization factory where SCARA-arm workcells with machine vision handle incoming paper records — separating folders and binders, finding and removing staples/fasteners, sorting and imaging pages, and classifying content — after which customers' paper is recycled/destroyed and the records live on in digital storage.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: bulk scan-and-dispose processing of retired paper records. It carries over because the physical objects (file folders, fastened paper packets, binders, mixed sizes) and the required precision (separating and handling individual sheets without tearing) are the same as a records purge, and the endpoint is the same — content moved to inactive (digital) storage and the paper sent for destruction/recycling. Only the retention decision differs, and that is a software rule applied to the item, not a physical act.

tasks.label: Assign and record or stamp identification numbers or codes to index materials for filing.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: High-volume back-office document prep/imaging unit (insurance claims, bank, healthcare billing, state agency): clerk takes incoming batches of loose paper, assigns batch and document control numbers, imprints or applies barcode cover sheets/labels on the paper, and records the numbers in the capture/index system.

Mailroom / records intake desk: incoming correspondence, forms, invoices and receipts are opened, date-stamped, and given sequential receipt or control numbers with a numbering stamp or label; numbers logged into a register or database before routing to files.

Chart/case-file folder identification in a clinic, hospital HIM department, or agency file room: clerk assigns the next medical record/case number, prints and affixes barcode and color-coded alpha/numeric labels to folder tabs, and records the number in the file-tracking index.

Law firm / litigation support: sequentially Bates-numbering or exhibit-stamping paper productions (hundreds to thousands of pages, mixed sizes, stapled sets), then recording the assigned number ranges in the production log/index.

Records center or archives accessioning: assigning accession, box and folder numbers to transferred records, applying printed barcode labels to cartons and folders on a work table, and recording box numbers and shelf locations in the inventory database.

Ad-hoc marking of odd or fragile media at the desk or in the stacks: hand-writing or affixing identification numbers on photographs, oversize drawings/plats, bound registers, X-ray jackets, or items already bound into binders and evidence packets, interleaved with other clerical duties.
